Translations.Title: Functions and Function Notation
Translations.Explanation:
Learning objectives: distinguish a function from a relation; evaluate values and equations using function notation; decide when a function is one-to-one; use vertical and horizontal line tests; and identify basic toolkit families and their domains.

Begin by listing ordered pairs and discussing the independent and dependent variables. Have learners test whether repeated inputs produce conflicting outputs. A repeated output alone does not violate the definition of a function.

Represent input-output rules with f(x). Interpret real-world input labels and numeric inputs, and make substitutions including x=−2, a and a+h. When solving f(x)=c, seek all permitted input values rather than evaluating f(c).

Compare tables, formulas and plotted points. Use vertical lines to test single-valuedness and horizontal lines to test whether the function is one-to-one. For implicit curves, inspect upper and lower branches separately.

Use graphical and tabular toolkit-family tasks: linear, square, cube, absolute-value, reciprocal, square-root, constant and identity. Record domain restrictions such as x≠0 for 1/x and x≥0 for √x.

Teacher-led activity: provide coordinate grids or a graphing tool. Ask learners to draw y=x², x=y² and y=|x|−1, sketch vertical and horizontal test lines, annotate all intersections, and justify results orally or in writing. Teacher validates hand-drawn scale and mathematical claims; these are not automatically scored.

Independent section practice can include verbal descriptions, algebraic relations, tables, graph classification, technology-assisted view windows and applied situations. Independent exercises, including table, algebra, graph, and applied tasks, must be discussed using their own models, units and stated input domains. A teacher checks graph drawings and written explanations.

Teacher checkpoint: compare an input/output mapping, a function evaluation, an inverse-direction ambiguity and two graph tests. Keep contextual units visible. Alternate representations must preserve the definition and intended domain; graph accuracy is a human review task until the display contract is exercised.

Independent Try It 1 — Classifying a pair of mappings. In a small library, book IDs A, B, C identify titles Alpha, Beta, Gamma without duplicates. Is title a function of book ID? Is book ID a function of title? Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 2 — Function notation in context. A plant's measured height h in centimetres depends on the day d since planting. Express this as a named function and state what h(8)=17 means. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 3 — Classification of a table. A table contains input/output pairs (1,10), (2,100), (3,1000). Decide whether this is a function and justify. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 4 — Evaluate an integer radical. For f(t)=sqrt(t-9), calculate f(13) and state the real domain. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 5 — Solve an integer radical equation. For f(t)=sqrt(t-9), find the input with output four. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 6 — Isolate a cubed dependent variable. Rewrite x=27y^3 as y=f(x) for real x. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 7 — Evaluate a table-encoded function. The table shows (0,6), (1,8), (2,10). Find g(1). Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 8 — Solve a function equation from a graph. On coordinate paper, graph f(x)=|x-1|, then identify each x at which f(x)=1. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 9 — Inverse direction in a contextual mapping. Each employee is assigned exactly one department, and at least two employees are assigned to the same department. Is department a function of employee? Is employee a function of department? Is the first function one-to-one? Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 10 — Contextual function versus injectivity. A score from 0 to 100 determines exactly one letter grade, and several scores share each letter. Is letter grade a function of numeric score? Is it one-to-one? Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 11 — Vertical-line test for a graph. Sketch y=|x| and explain whether each vertical line meets its graph in at most one point. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 12 — A prerequisite to injectivity. Inspect the independent circle x²+y²=4: at x=0 the relation has outputs y=2 and y=−2, so it fails the vertical-line test and cannot be a one-to-one function. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Instructor-graded graphical practice (source Section 1.1, exercises 52–59): learners read labelled axes, distinguish a graph that fails the vertical-line test from one that merely fails one-to-one, and justify every horizontal-line intersection. An original source graph beginning near (−2,0) shows f(−1)≈1; its displayed right-hand curve does not establish an exact input for f(x)=3, so students must label any extrapolated value as an estimate. Follow the separate teacher rubric; these diagrams and explanations have no proven automatic grader or production delivery.

Edulytics cool-down: given R={(1,2),(1,4),(2,4)}, classify R and explain; evaluate f(−1) for f(x)=x²−2x+1; and decide whether h(x)=x² is one-to-one when x≥0. Submit reasons. A teacher reviews the explanation; this cool-down is independently authored, not a reproduction of teacher-restricted material.

First-party supplemental example — overlapping horizontal-ray domains. For y=3 when x>0 and y=−3 when x<2, the two rules overlap for 0<x<2. At x=1 the relation contains both (1,3) and (1,−3); it fails the vertical-line test. Explain this with labelled axes. This is an Edulytics original illustration, not the original publisher graphic.

First-party table for worked example 11: x inputs −1, 0, 1, 2 correspond respectively to f(x) values 4, 1, 4, 9. Read f(0)=1. To solve f(x)=4 from the table, report both displayed inputs, x=−1 and x=1. The table alone cannot determine outputs for unlisted inputs.

Tables for Section 1.1: each input can have exactly one output while several distinct inputs may share a result. The 14 first-party source-skill table representations include menu/grade interpretation, nonnumeric inputs, tabulated function tests, month/day values, lookup and inverted lookup, basic toolkit families, and the Section exercise table. Inspect all original axes, figure captions and source table numerals separately when grading original exercises.

Notation choice — in applied mathematics one may write y=y(x). For introductory function analysis, y=f(x) distinguishes the function rule f from the output value y, so treat them as different mathematical roles.

Implicit function subtlety — an equation can determine one output for each input without giving an easy explicit formula for that output. Test uniqueness of the output branch; conversely, equations such as a circle may produce two real y-values for the same x and are not functions of x.

Function notation uses parentheses to indicate the INPUT to a function, not multiplication: f(a+b) applies f after determining a+b as one complete input.

A table can list every known pair or selected observations from a wider relationship. A few sampled ordered pairs do not determine how the function behaves outside the table.

A graph may consist of isolated plotted values for a discrete domain, or the complete curve representing all ordered pairs in a continuous domain. Plotting sampled points alone does not prove continuity between them.

The nine basic toolkit-function families are constant, identity, absolute value, quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, reciprocal squared, square root, and cube root. For reciprocal and reciprocal squared exclude x=0; the square root has real x>=0.

Independent example input-output samples for nine basic families: constant 2: D(-2)=D(0)=D(2)=2; identity maps -2,0,2 to -2,0,2; absolute value maps -2,0,2 to 2,0,2; quadratic -2,-1,0,1,2 to 4,1,0,1,4; cubic -1,-0.5,0,0.5,1 to -1,-0.125,0,0.125,1; reciprocal -2,-1,-0.5,0.5,1,2 to -0.5,-1,-2,2,1,0.5; reciprocal squared to 0.25,1,4,4,1,0.25; square root 0,1,4 to 0,1,2; and cube root -1,-0.125,0,0.125,1 to -1,-0.5,0,0.5,1. Exclude input 0 from reciprocal families; use nonnegative inputs for real square roots.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Relation, domain and range: A relation is a set of ordered input-output pairs; its domain contains inputs and its range contains outputs.
Rule: An x or other input can occur more than once, but a function forbids conflicting outputs for that input.
Example: {(1,2),(2,4),(2,4)} is a function.

Definition of a function: Each allowed input is assigned exactly one output.
Rule: To disprove a function, exhibit an input paired with two distinct outputs.
Example: {(1,2),(1,3)} is not a function.

Function notation and dependent quantity: f(x) names the output produced by f on input x; inputs can be labels as well as numbers.
Rule: Evaluate f(a) by substituting a for every occurrence of the input.
Example: f(x)=x²+1 gives f(−2)=5.

Evaluating a function expression: An input such as a+h must be treated as one substituted object.
Rule: For f(x)=x², f(a+h)=(a+h)²=a²+2ah+h², not a²+h².
Example: f(x)=x²+3x−4 implies [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h=2a+h+3 when h≠0.

Solving for an input: Solving f(x)=c asks which input values yield output c.
Rule: Set the function expression equal to c and solve, testing domain restrictions.
Example: p²+2p=3 yields p=1 or p=−3.

One-to-one (injective): A function is one-to-one when different inputs never have the same output.
Rule: f(a)=f(b) implies a=b, with the specified domain.
Example: r↦πr² is one-to-one for r≥0.

Vertical and horizontal graph tests: Vertical-line intersections test whether y is a function of x; horizontal-line intersections test one-to-one.
Rule: No vertical line may meet a function graph twice; no horizontal line may meet a one-to-one function graph twice.
Example: y=x² passes vertical but fails horizontal.

Basic function families: Toolkit graphs include constant, identity, square, cube, absolute value, reciprocal, square root and related transformations.
Rule: Graph shape, domain and function notation must be understood together; reciprocal excludes x=0 and square root requires x≥0.
Example: f(x)=1/x is undefined at 0; g(x)=√x is real for x≥0.

Basic toolkit function families: Nine toolkit families: constant, identity, absolute value, quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, reciprocal squared, square root, and cube root. Read formula, graph, domain and range together: 1/x and 1/x² exclude x=0, while √x requires x≥0.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
1. Can an item determine its price?
Task: A ticket desk sells adult tickets for $12, student tickets for $8, and senior tickets for $8. Is ticket price a function of ticket category? Is category a function of price?
Method: Check whether each input is associated with exactly one output.
Step 1: For category-to-price, each of adult, student and senior has exactly one displayed dollar amount.
Step 2: For price-to-category, the $8 input corresponds to two categories: student and senior.
Step 3: Therefore category-to-price is a function, while price-to-category is not.
Answer: Price is a function of category; category is not a function of price.
Check: Repeated output values are allowed for a function; repeated inputs with distinct outputs are not.

2. Classify a grade-band rule
Task: Suppose percentages 78–86 map to GPA 3.0 and 87–91 map to GPA 3.5. Is GPA a function of percentage? Is percentage a function of GPA?
Method: Treat the input-to-output rule as a mapping, not an average.
Step 1: Every percentage in the specified bands has one GPA according to the table.
Step 2: Many percentages, such as 80 and 85, both map to GPA 3.0.
Step 3: Thus GPA depends functionally on percentage, while reversing the direction is not single-valued.
Answer: GPA is a function of percentage; percentage is not a function of GPA.
Check: For the inverse direction, GPA 3.0 has more than one possible percentage.

3. Express a nonnumeric input in function notation
Task: The number of scheduled stops depends on the bus route. Route A has 7 stops and route B has 12. Express these facts using function notation.
Method: Identify the independent variable before naming the function.
Step 1: Take the route label as input r and its number of stops as output.
Step 2: Define s(r) as the number of stops assigned to route r.
Step 3: Evaluate at the named routes.
Answer: s(A)=7 and s(B)=12.
Check: The input is a route label; it does not need to be a number.

4. Interpret a function-value statement
Task: Let N(y) be the number of employees of a company in year y. Explain N(2024)=135.
Method: Read the input and output in context.
Step 1: Identify 2024 as the input year.
Step 2: Identify N(y) as a headcount rather than a year or dollar amount.
Step 3: State the observation using the correct units.
Answer: In 2024 the company employed 135 people.
Check: Do not confuse the input year with the output headcount.

5. Determine whether a table is a function
Task: Compare three independently authored relation tables. Table A: (2,1),(5,3),(8,6). Table B: (-3,5),(0,1),(4,5). Table C: (1,0),(5,2),(5,4). Classify whether EACH table defines y as a function of x; for the functional tables decide whether one-to-one, with reasons.
Method: Check each input and its output independently in all three tables; then test repeated outputs.
Step 1: Table A has three distinct inputs and three distinct outputs: it is a one-to-one function.
Step 2: Table B has distinct inputs, but -3 and 4 both map to 5: it is a function but not one-to-one.
Step 3: Table C maps the same input 5 to both 2 and 4: it is not a function at all.
Answer: Table A: one-to-one function. Table B: function but not one-to-one. Table C: not a function.
Check: A repeated output is allowed for a function; a repeated input with a conflicting output is not.

6. Evaluate and simplify an input expression
Task: For f(x)=x²+3x−4, calculate f(2), f(a), f(a+h), and [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h for h≠0.
Method: Substitute the entire input before expanding.
Step 1: Evaluate at x=2: f(2)=4+6−4=6.
Step 2: Evaluate at symbolic input a: f(a)=a²+3a−4.
Step 3: At input a+h, f(a+h)=(a+h)²+3(a+h)−4=a²+2ah+h²+3a+3h−4.
Step 4: For h≠0, subtract f(a) from f(a+h), factor h, then simplify the difference quotient to 2a+h+3.
Answer: f(2)=6; f(a)=a²+3a−4; f(a+h)=a²+2ah+h²+3a+3h−4; quotient=2a+h+3.
Check: The quotient expression requires h≠0.

7. Evaluate at a numeric input
Task: Given h(p)=p²+2p, evaluate h(4).
Method: Replace every p with 4 and respect order of operations.
Step 1: Write h(4)=4²+2(4).
Step 2: Calculate 4²=16 and 2(4)=8.
Step 3: Add the terms to obtain 24.
Answer: 24
Check: 16+8=24, not 36.

8. Solve a function-value equation
Task: For h(p)=p²+2p, find all inputs p for which h(p)=3.
Method: Equate the function output to 3 and solve the quadratic.
Step 1: Set p²+2p=3, or p²+2p−3=0.
Step 2: Factor (p+3)(p−1)=0.
Step 3: Check p=−3 and p=1 in h.
Answer: p=−3 or p=1.
Check: h(−3)=9−6=3 and h(1)=1+2=3.

9. Isolate an output variable
Task: Rewrite 2n+6p=12 as p=f(n).
Method: Isolate p using equation-preserving operations.
Step 1: Subtract 2n: 6p=12−2n.
Step 2: Divide all terms by 6: p=(12−2n)/6.
Step 3: Simplify the two terms.
Answer: p=f(n)=2−n/3.
Check: Substituting gives 2n+6(2−n/3)=12.

10. Why the unit circle is not a y-function
Task: Does x²+y²=1 specify one value of y for every x on [−1,1]?
Method: Identify when one x has more than one y.
Step 1: At x=0, the equation becomes y²=1.
Step 2: Both y=1 and y=−1 satisfy the relation.
Step 3: Without a branch restriction, the relation fails to specify a single y value.
Answer: No. The upper branch y=√(1−x²) and lower branch y=−√(1−x²) separately define functions on [−1,1].
Check: The two points (0,1) and (0,−1) have the same input.

11. Read and solve from tabulated values
Task: A table gives f(−1)=4, f(0)=1, f(1)=4, f(2)=9. Evaluate f(0) and find every table input with f(x)=4.
Method: Read values from recorded ordered pairs.
Step 1: Locate x=0 and read its listed output 1.
Step 2: Scan the output column for 4.
Step 3: Report both input values −1 and 1.
Answer: f(0)=1; the listed solutions of f(x)=4 are x=−1 and x=1.
Check: Do not assume these are the only solutions outside the given table.

12. Extract values from a graph description
Task: A plotted V-shaped graph represents f(x)=|x|−1. Find f(−2) and all x with f(x)=2.
Method: Translate the graph to the equivalent absolute-value rule.
Step 1: Read f(−2)=|−2|−1=1.
Step 2: Solve |x|−1=2, giving |x|=3.
Step 3: Use both branches of the absolute value equation.
Answer: f(−2)=1; x=−3 or x=3.
Check: A graph horizontal line y=2 intersects this V shape twice.

13. Area as a one-to-one function of radius
Task: Is the area of a circular disk a function of radius r≥0? Is it one-to-one on this domain?
Method: Use the area formula and the physical domain.
Step 1: Set A(r)=πr² with r≥0.
Step 2: Every nonnegative radius has exactly one area.
Step 3: For nonnegative radii, larger r gives strictly larger area, so equal areas require equal radii.
Answer: Yes, A is a function and is one-to-one for r≥0.
Check: Without r≥0, r and −r would share the same area; domain matters.

14. Apply the vertical-line test
Task: Apply the vertical-line test to three independent model graphs: (A) y=x², (B) y=2x+1, and (C) y²=x. Which of A, B, C represent y as a function of x, and why?
Method: Check whether a vertical line can hit the graph more than once.
Step 1: A: each real x has one output x², so every vertical line meets the parabola at most once.
Step 2: B: each real x has exactly one output 2x+1, so a nonvertical straight line passes.
Step 3: C: at x=4 the sideways relation contains both (4,2) and (4,-2), so it fails.
Answer: Graphs A and B are functions of x. Graph C is not a function of x.
Check: The test concerns the number of outputs for a SINGLE x; it is not a test of injectivity.

15. Apply the horizontal-line test
Task: Compare f(x)=(x−1)² and g(x)=2x−1 on all real inputs. Which functions are one-to-one?
Method: Look for repeated outputs at different x values.
Step 1: f(0)=1 and f(2)=1, so one horizontal line intersects f twice.
Step 2: If g(a)=g(b), then 2a−1=2b−1 forces a=b.
Step 3: Therefore the linear nonconstant g is one-to-one and the parabola f is not.
Answer: g(x)=2x−1 is one-to-one; f(x)=(x−1)² is not.
Check: Restricting f to x≥1 would make it one-to-one, but that is a different domain.

16. Two horizontal rays with overlapping input domains
Task: A relation is formed from two horizontal rays: y=3 when x>0 and y=−3 when x<2. Is the relation y=f(x)? Justify your answer using a vertical line.
Method: Check where the two permitted input domains overlap, rather than treating each ray in isolation.
Step 1: The upper ray includes all x>0, while the lower ray includes all x<2.
Step 2: Both rules apply to every input with 0<x<2.
Step 3: Choose x=1. The relation includes (1,3) and (1,−3), so a vertical line x=1 intersects it twice.
Answer: No. The combined relation is not a function of x: for every x in (0,2) there are two distinct outputs.
Check: Whether a ray has an open endpoint does not matter if the rays' input domains overlap elsewhere.

Translations.CommonMistakes:
Treating a repeated output as evidence that a relation is not a function.
Why incorrect: Many different inputs may lead to one output.
Correction: Check whether any one input has two distinct outputs.

Computing f(a+h) as f(a)+f(h) without justification.
Why incorrect: Functions generally do not distribute across addition of inputs.
Correction: Substitute the full expression a+h into the defining formula.

Answering f(x)=3 by substituting x=3.
Why incorrect: The problem asks for an input that produces output 3, not for f(3).
Correction: Solve the equation f(x)=3 and check the solutions.

Using the horizontal-line test to decide whether a relation is a function.
Why incorrect: Horizontal-line test checks injectivity, not single-valuedness.
Correction: First apply vertical-line test; only then apply horizontal-line test.

Calling a circle graph y=f(x) without a branch restriction.
Why incorrect: A single x can have both positive and negative y solutions.
Correction: Select upper or lower semicircle and state the domain.

Assuming a pair of separate horizontal rays automatically passes the vertical-line test.
Why incorrect: Two separate pieces can give different y-values for the same x if their input domains overlap.
Correction: Write the x-domain of each piece and test their intersection; for the two-ray example any x in (0,2) yields two y-values.
Translations.QuickSummary:
A function assigns exactly one output to every allowed input.
Repeated inputs are permitted only when their outputs agree.
f(x) is the output at input x; f(x)=c asks for possible inputs.
One-to-one means distinct inputs have distinct outputs.
Vertical-line test checks function status; horizontal-line test checks one-to-one status.
Toolkit functions require correct domains, graph shapes and units.
Open-ended graph interpretation and written proof are teacher-reviewed.
Two separate graph pieces can still fail to define a function when their input domains overlap and assign different outputs.

Translations.Title: Domain and Range
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: determine domains for finite mappings and functions defined by formulas, convert unions and exclusions to interval and set-builder notation, read domain and range from graphs, and evaluate or graph piecewise functions.

Find the domain before computing outputs. For a polynomial every real input is permitted; for a rational function solve its denominator equal to zero and exclude those inputs; for an even root enforce a nonnegative radicand.

Parentheses exclude finite endpoints and brackets include them. Use ∪ to combine intervals and use a parenthesis with each infinite endpoint.

An isolated graph point contributes a specific input and output. A continuous curve contributes an interval of inputs and attained outputs. A source figure may be an observed data window, not proof about values outside it.

To determine range of a quadratic, identify its turning point and direction; to determine range of an odd-degree cubic with opposite end limits, recognize all real outputs; to determine range of a reciprocal, exclude any unattainable output.

A piecewise rule partitions inputs by strict or inclusive inequalities. Label open/closed circles and evaluate exactly one branch at a permitted input.

Context restricts mathematical domains: positive integer group sizes, a finite series of calendar years, real measurement units, or nonnegative flight height can exclude values that the algebra alone allows.

Teacher-led source-skill activity: compare domain and range on independent coordinate diagrams for reciprocal, radical, and multi-branch functions. Verify units, endpoint membership and graph axes manually.

Independent Try It practice contains eight independently authored tasks covering original Section 1.2 learner actions. Teachers assess graph constructions and open-ended reasoning.

Independent Try It 1 — Finite domain set. A mapping includes (−6,2),(0,5),(4,2),(9,8). Write its domain.

Independent Try It 2 — Polynomial domain. Find the real domain of F(x)=x⁵−2x²+4.

Independent Try It 3 — Rational restriction. Find the domain of f(x)=(3x+1)/(5x−4).

Independent Try It 4 — Root restriction. Find the domain of g(x)=√(3x+12).

Independent Try It 5 — Real interval descriptions. Write −3<x≤1 or x≥5 in interval notation.

Independent Try It 6 — Domain and range of a sampled function. At discrete years 2019,2020,2021,2022 the observed metric is 20,45,30,50. Give the observed input and output sets.

Independent Try It 7 — Radical range. For h(x)=−√(8−x), find real domain and range.

Independent Try It 8 — Piecewise with missing endpoints. Graph f(x)=x² if x<−1, f(x)=1 if −1<x<2 and f(x)=√(x−2) if x>2. State the domain and open endpoint behavior.

Independent Edulytics cool-down — (a) State the domain of f(x)=(x+1)/(x−2). (b) Give domain and range of g(x)=−√(9−x). (c) For h(x)=x+2 when x<0 and h(x)=x−1 when x≥0, evaluate h(0) and explain which point is closed. Submit separate rational-domain, radical-range and piecewise-endpoint explanations for teacher assessment.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Domain and range
The domain contains permitted input values and the range contains attained outputs.
Read allowed x-values first; then identify all outputs actually attained.
For (2,9),(3,9),(4,10), domain is {2,3,4} and range {9,10}.

Interval notation
Parentheses omit finite endpoints and brackets include them.
Infinity is never included; unions combine disjoint allowed sets.
x<1 or x≥4 corresponds to (−∞,1)∪[4,∞).

Algebraic domain restriction
Polynomials accept all real inputs; rational denominators cannot vanish.
Even-root radicands must be nonnegative; root denominators must be strictly positive.
√(x−5) needs x≥5, while 1/√(x−5) needs x>5.

Graph-derived domain and range
Horizontal coverage yields domain, and vertical coverage yields range.
Distinguish discrete points, continuous curves, open/closed endpoints and plotted windows.
y=|x−1|−2 has all-real domain and range [−2,∞).

Toolkit shapes
Quadratic ranges may be bounded below; cubic ranges cover ℝ; reciprocals omit a value.
Analyze each exact rule and branch rather than assume a picture's drawn window is full domain.
4/(x−2) omits x=2 and output 0.

Piecewise functions
A piecewise function uses more than one formula on disjoint input conditions.
At each boundary apply only the permitted condition; annotate included and excluded endpoint points.
f(x)=x² for x≤0 and f(x)=1 for x>0 gives f(0)=0.

Applied domain and units
Real context can constrain otherwise unrestricted mathematical formulas.
Nonnegative quantities, integer counts, dates and physical units limit contextual domains.
h(t)=−16t²+96t describes nonnegative height during t∈[0,6].
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Finite domain of a tabulated relation
A function has the finite pairs {(1,11),(3,11),(5,15),(8,20)}. List its domain as a set.
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: {1,3,5,8}

Example 2: All-real polynomial domain
Find the domain of the polynomial F(x)=2x³−x+7 in interval notation.
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: (−∞,∞)

Example 3: Domain excluding a denominator zero
Determine the real domain of R(x)=(x+4)/(x−3).
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: (−∞,3)∪(3,∞)

Example 4: Domain of an even root
Find the domain of S(x)=√(11−2x).
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: (−∞,11/2]

Example 5: Open and closed interval unions
Describe the independent real set −1≤x≤2 or x>4 using set-builder and interval notation.
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: {x∈ℝ | −1≤x≤2 or x>4}; [−1,2]∪(4,∞)

Example 6: Finite graph domain and range with open and closed endpoints
An independent parabola segment follows f(x)=(x+1)²−4 only for −3<x≤1. Plot it with correct open/filled boundary points and find its domain and range.
Method: Use the stated function restriction for domain and the vertex and attained endpoints for range.
Answer: Domain (−3,1]; range [−4,0].

Example 7: Observed continuous interpolation has a bounded domain and range
A first-party environmental metric is recorded in tons/day for 2018–2023: 120,150,180,130,220,200. Model a CHART by connecting consecutive annual points with straight line segments. Read the domain and range of the displayed interpolation, and distinguish them from data outside the window.
Method: The sampled annual values are given; a continuous interpolation is explicitly defined only between sampled years.
Answer: Displayed interpolation: domain [2018,2023] years; range [120,220] tons/day.

Example 8: Domain and range of a cubic
Find domain and range of f(x)=x³−4x.
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: Domain (−∞,∞); range (−∞,∞)

Example 9: Reciprocal domain and range
For f(x)=4/(x−2), find the real domain and range.
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: Domain (−∞,2)∪(2,∞); range (−∞,0)∪(0,∞)

Example 10: Radical domain and range
Find domain and range of f(x)=3√(x+1).
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: Domain [−1,∞); range [0,∞)

Example 11: Construct an integer-input piecewise cost rule
A tour costs $6 per participant for groups of 1–7 and a flat $48 for groups of 8 or more. Write C(n).
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: C(n)=6n for integers 1≤n≤7; C(n)=48 for integers n≥8.

Example 12: Evaluate two piecewise pricing intervals
Let P(g)=20 for 0<g<3 and P(g)=20+8(g−3) for g≥3. Find P(2) and P(5).
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: P(2)=20; P(5)=36

Example 13: Graph a three-piece definition with endpoints
Let f(x)=x² for x≤0, f(x)=2 for 0<x≤3, and f(x)=x−1 for x>3. Identify open and closed endpoints, domain, and whether the graph is a function.
Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Answer: Domain (−∞,∞); the graph is a function. At x=0, f(0)=0; at x=3, f(3)=2.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions:
1. Finite domain of a tabulated relation
Step 1: Keep only first coordinates, since inputs define the domain.
Step 2: Remove duplicates without changing the input values.
Step 3: Validate: The repeated output 11 does not change the domain.

2. All-real polynomial domain
Step 1: Powers with whole-number exponents exist at every real input.
Step 2: No denominator or even radical restricts x.
Step 3: Validate: Substitute any real number; the polynomial is defined.

3. Domain excluding a denominator zero
Step 1: Solve the forbidden denominator condition x−3=0.
Step 2: Remove 3 from the real line and use an open endpoint on both sides.
Step 3: Validate: x=3 would divide by zero.

4. Domain of an even root
Step 1: Enforce 11−2x≥0.
Step 2: Solve −2x≥−11, reversing the inequality when dividing by a negative.
Step 3: Validate: The endpoint x=11/2 gives zero and is included.

5. Open and closed interval unions
Step 1: The first component includes both −1 and 2.
Step 2: The second component excludes 4 and has no finite upper endpoint.
Step 3: Validate: Brackets include, parentheses exclude; infinity always uses a parenthesis.

6. Finite graph domain and range with open and closed endpoints
Step 1: The x-window is −3<x≤1, so the domain is (−3,1].
Step 2: The left endpoint would be (−3,0), but it is OPEN because x=−3 is excluded.
Step 3: The vertex (−1,−4) is included and gives the smallest output.
Step 4: The right endpoint (1,0) is included, so 0 is in the range despite the excluded left endpoint.

7. Observed continuous interpolation has a bounded domain and range
Step 1: Label x as year (2018–2023) and y as metric (tons/day); connect consecutive points only inside that closed window.
Step 2: Under the explicitly specified piecewise-linear interpolation, every time t from 2018 to 2023 has one output.
Step 3: The observed and interpolated minimum is 120 and maximum is 220 tons/day.
Step 4: Do not infer that the actual process has those bounds before 2018 or after 2023.

8. Domain and range of a cubic
Step 1: The polynomial is defined for all real x.
Step 2: As x→∞ the cubic grows without bound; as x→−∞ it decreases without bound.
Step 3: Validate: Continuity and unbounded opposite end behavior yield every real output.

9. Reciprocal domain and range
Step 1: The denominator x−2 cannot equal zero, so x≠2.
Step 2: Because the numerator is nonzero, the output cannot equal zero; every other real y occurs for x=2+4/y.
Step 3: Validate: Check x=2 undefined and f(x)=0 impossible.

10. Radical domain and range
Step 1: Require x+1≥0, so x≥−1.
Step 2: The principal square root is nonnegative, so multiplying by 3 preserves outputs y≥0.
Step 3: Validate: At x=−1 the value is zero and larger inputs yield arbitrarily large outputs.

11. Construct an integer-input piecewise cost rule
Step 1: People counts n must be positive integers.
Step 2: For 1≤n≤7, use C(n)=6n.
Step 3: For n≥8, use C(n)=48.

12. Evaluate two piecewise pricing intervals
Step 1: Since 2<3, P(2)=20.
Step 2: Since 5≥3, P(5)=20+8(2)=36.
Step 3: Validate: At g=3 the second branch applies and gives 20.

13. Graph a three-piece definition with endpoints
Step 1: At x=0 use the quadratic branch, with filled (0,0) and open (0,2).
Step 2: At x=3 use the constant branch, with filled (3,2); the last segment begins just right of 3.
Step 3: Each x belongs to exactly one branch, and the combined domain covers every real x.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Using a bracket at a value that makes a denominator zero.
Why: Division by zero is undefined.
Correction: Solve the denominator-zero equation and exclude roots with open interval boundaries.

Treating an odd root as if it were an even root.
Why: Odd roots accept negative real radicands.
Correction: Only even radicals demand a nonnegative radicand.

Reporting domain alone when asked for range.
Why: Range refers to attained output values, not permitted inputs.
Correction: Study y-values using the function rule, not only its input restrictions.

Connecting discrete annual observations with unproved continuous values.
Why: Recorded points do not certify intermediate or extrapolated outputs.
Correction: Identify the observation domain separately from a supplied continuous model.

Applying two piecewise branches to the same boundary input.
Why: The inequalities allocate inputs between branches.
Correction: Choose the branch whose boundary condition actually contains the input.

Using a closed dot at an omitted piecewise endpoint.
Why: A strict inequality excludes that endpoint.
Correction: Open circles mean excluded; filled circles mean included.

Using an included branch boundary to assign two different values at the same x.
Why: A piecewise function must have a single active formula at every permitted input.
Correction: Before evaluating a boundary, check exactly one inequality; a strict endpoint uses an open circle.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. A domain is the complete set of permitted inputs, whereas the range consists of attained outputs.

2. Exclude zeros of rational denominators; include an even-root boundary when the radicand is zero unless it also lies in a denominator.

3. Use parentheses for omitted endpoints, brackets for included endpoints, and unions for separated intervals.

4. A graph's input and output extents can be discrete, bounded or unbounded.

5. For piecewise rules select one branch by its inequality and mark open or filled endpoints.

6. Use physical contexts and units to narrow an algebraically permitted domain.

7. Independent open-ended graph reasoning is teacher-assessed, not automatically graded.

Translations.Title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: calculate average rates from tables, formulas and plotted endpoints, interpret change signs and physical units, identify increasing/decreasing/constant intervals, estimate local extrema and distinguish them from absolute extrema.

Secant slope between a<b is Δy/Δx=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a). Use the same input order for both differences; use output-units per input-units.

A positive rate describes increasing net output over an interval; a negative rate describes decreasing net output. A local slope may vary inside the interval.

Increasing/decreasing intervals describe behavior reading the graph from left to right, not whether y is positive or negative. Report open input intervals around turning points when appropriate.

Local extrema depend on a neighborhood; absolute extrema compare all permitted inputs. Always state the graph's domain, including any open endpoints and asymptotes.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down — (a) Compute average change of h(t)=t²+2t from t=1 to t=4. (b) Classify increasing/decreasing intervals for f(x)=x² on ℝ. (c) Explain why an increasing graph may have a negative output.

Independent Try It 1 — Compute a rate from recorded prices. A fare rises from $2.20 in 2019 to $2.80 in 2023. Find the average change per year.

Independent Try It 2 — Average rate with a radical. For f(x)=x−2√x, compute average rate on [1,9].

Independent Try It 3 — Symbolic average rate. For f(x)=x²+2x−8 find average rate on [5,a] with a≠5.

Independent Try It 4 — Use local extrema to classify monotonicity. Graph f(x)=x³−6x²−15x+20. Approximate the two local extrema and increasing/decreasing intervals.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Average rate of change
The secant slope between inputs a and b is (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a).
Use the SAME ordered endpoints in numerator and denominator.
f(2)=7 and f(5)=1 implies average rate −2.

Rate units and sign
A change in output per one input unit has output-units/input-units.
Negative average rate means outputs fall as inputs increase across the interval.
Dollars per year and miles per hour are different units.

Increasing, decreasing and constant
Increasing means outputs rise as x moves right; decreasing means outputs fall; constant means no change.
Monotonic intervals are input intervals, not output ranges.
y=x² is decreasing for x<0 and increasing for x>0.

Local extrema
A local maximum/minimum is the highest/lowest value among nearby inputs in the domain.
Local extrema do not necessarily dominate all values in the full domain.
x³−3x has local maximum 2 at x=−1 and local minimum −2 at x=1.

Absolute extrema
The absolute maximum/minimum is greatest/least output over the ENTIRE given domain.
A bounded domain can attain its extremum at a boundary; an unbounded curve might not attain an absolute maximum.
The bounded graph with outputs −10..16 attains both absolute extremes.

Domain-aware graphical reasoning
A continuous graph may have turning points, jumps, asymptotes and clipped viewing windows.
Do not infer global extrema from a clipped plot, and do not join intervals across excluded x.
For 3/x+x/2, never combine monotonicity across x=0.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Average change in a time series
An independently collected annual cost series rises from $2.50 per unit in 2020 to $3.10 per unit in 2024. Find average change per year.
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: $0.15 per unit per year

Example 2: Average slope from two plotted points
A plotted continuous function passes through (−1,4) and (2,1). Compute average rate on [−1,2].
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: −1 output unit per input unit

Example 3: Average speed from measured distance
A vehicle's distance from the starting position changes from 6 miles at t=0 hours to 276 miles at t=6 hours. Find average speed.
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: 45 miles per hour

Example 4: Average change from a formula
For f(x)=x²−2/x, find the average rate over [2,4].
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: 25/4

Example 5: Average inverse-square force change
A hypothetical force obeys F(d)=6/d² newtons for distance d>0 cm. Find the average force change over [2,6].
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: −1/3 newton per centimeter

Example 6: Symbolic endpoint rate
For g(t)=t²+4t+2, compute the average change from t=0 to t=a, a≠0.
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: a+4, for a≠0

Example 7: Monotonic intervals from a graph
A continuous graph rises over (1,3), falls over (3,4) and rises again for t>4. Identify all increasing intervals.
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: (1,3) and (4,∞)

Example 8: Local extrema of a rational-plus-linear rule
For f(x)=3/x+x/2, x≠0, locate local extrema and intervals of increasing/decreasing.
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: Local maximum (−√6,−√6); local minimum (√6,√6). Increasing (−∞,−√6) and (√6,∞); decreasing (−√6,0) and (0,√6).

Example 9: Local extrema from an independently specified cubic
For f(x)=x³−3x, identify local extrema and their values.
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: Local maximum at (−1,2); local minimum at (1,−2).

Example 10: Absolute extrema on a complete displayed bounded model
Connect successive independent graph points (−3,0),(−2,16),(−1,10),(0,0),(1,10),(2,16),(3,−10) with straight segments over [−3,3]. Find absolute max/min.
Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Answer: Absolute maximum 16 attained at x=−2 and x=2; absolute minimum −10 at x=3.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions:
1. Average change in a time series
Step 1: The dependent value changes by $0.60.
Step 2: The year input changes by four years.
Step 3: Average rate is $0.60/4 years.

2. Average slope from two plotted points
Step 1: Read both endpoint coordinates.
Step 2: Compute Δy=1−4=−3.
Step 3: Compute Δx=2−(−1)=3 and divide.

3. Average speed from measured distance
Step 1: Total distance change=276−6=270 miles.
Step 2: Elapsed time=6 hours.
Step 3: Rate=270/6=45 miles per hour.

4. Average change from a formula
Step 1: f(2)=4−1=3.
Step 2: f(4)=16−1/2=31/2.
Step 3: Divide (31/2−3) by 2.

5. Average inverse-square force change
Step 1: F(2)=6/4=3/2 newtons.
Step 2: F(6)=6/36=1/6 newton.
Step 3: Rate=(1/6−3/2)/4=−1/3 newton/cm.

6. Symbolic endpoint rate
Step 1: g(a)=a²+4a+2 and g(0)=2.
Step 2: Divide a²+4a by a.
Step 3: Factor a and cancel only because a≠0.

7. Monotonic intervals from a graph
Step 1: Read graph direction left to right.
Step 2: Increasing where output rises, not where the graph lies above x-axis.
Step 3: Exclude turning-point boundaries under conventional open interval reporting.

8. Local extrema of a rational-plus-linear rule
Step 1: The derivative for x≠0 is −3/x²+1/2.
Step 2: Stationary inputs satisfy x²=6, giving x=±√6.
Step 3: The derivative is positive where |x|>√6 and negative where 0<|x|<√6.

9. Local extrema from an independently specified cubic
Step 1: Derivative f'(x)=3x²−3 vanishes at x=−1 and x=1.
Step 2: Sign changes from positive to negative at −1, and negative to positive at 1.
Step 3: Evaluate f(−1)=2 and f(1)=−2.

10. Absolute extrema on a complete displayed bounded model
Step 1: All seven points and connecting segments lie in the declared domain [−3,3].
Step 2: The greatest displayed output is 16 at two inputs −2 and 2.
Step 3: The least displayed output is −10 at the right included endpoint x=3.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Reversing only the denominator endpoints in a secant slope.
Why: This reverses the sign incorrectly.
Correction: Use (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a) consistently.

Interpreting a negative output as a decreasing function.
Why: The sign of f(x) and the direction of change are different properties.
Correction: Compare outputs as input increases.

Treating a local maximum as an absolute maximum on ℝ.
Why: A graph can rise higher outside the local neighborhood.
Correction: State domain and compare all outputs before claiming absolute.

Connecting increasing intervals across an excluded input.
Why: An asymptote separates the permitted domain into distinct pieces.
Correction: Report separate intervals around a missing input.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Average rate of change equals output change divided by input change; units are output units per input unit.

2. Use the same two endpoints in the numerator and denominator of the secant slope.

3. Increasing/decreasing/constant intervals depend on the graph's direction, not the sign of the output.

4. Local extrema describe a neighborhood; absolute extrema compare every permitted output.

5. Use domain restrictions and included endpoints when reasoning about global extrema.

6. First-party graph sketches and open-ended extrema are teacher-reviewed in Stage C.

Translations.Title: Composition of Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: combine function values by arithmetic, interpret composition as an ordered mapping, evaluate composite functions with tables, graphs and formulas, determine composite domains, and decompose a rule into inner and outer functions.

The quotient f/g requires x in the domains of both factors and g(x)≠0. Removing a symbolic factor cannot restore a forbidden input.

The composition (f∘g)(x) evaluates inner g then outer f, and generally differs from (g∘f)(x). The same procedure holds for chained tables and graphs: verify each intermediate input exists.

Composite domains depend on restrictions of g and on whether its outputs lie in the allowable input domain of f. Always test both layers.

Applied composition must have meaningful quantities and compatible units across the inner-output/outer-input interface.

A composite can be decomposed into two functions; multiple decompositions may exist, but they must reproduce the original formula and domain.

Edulytics independent cooldown: (a) Given f(x)=1/(x−2) and g(x)=x+1, find f(g(x)) and its domain. (b) Give a pair of simple functions for which f∘g and g∘f differ. (c) Explain why a quotient's removable factor does not restore the excluded input.

Independent Try It 1 — Operations and original quotient domain. With f(x)=x−2 and g(x)=x²−4, find (fg)(x), (f−g)(x), and their domains.

Independent Try It 2 — Unit-compatible composition. Let G(r) be gravitational force for orbital distance r and a(F) acceleration caused by force F. Form the physically meaningful composition.

Independent Try It 3 — Nested table lookups. Let f(1)=6,f(2)=5,f(3)=2,f(4)=7 and g(1)=3,g(2)=4,g(3)=1,g(4)=2. Find f(g(1)) and g(f(3)).

Independent Try It 4 — Graph composition with labelled points. An independent plot gives f(2)=4 and g(4)=1. Find g(f(2)).

Independent Try It 5 — Two numerical compositions. For f(x)=x²−2x and h(x)=2x+3, evaluate h(f(2)) and h(f(−2)).

Independent Try It 6 — Nested square root and reciprocal domain. Let f(x)=1/(x−3) and g(x)=√(x+2). Find domain of f(g(x)).

Independent Try It 7 — Construct inside and outside expressions. Decompose H(x)=4/(5−√(x²+2)) into an inner and outer function and state its domain.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Function arithmetic
Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division combine output values pointwise.
The quotient domain is the common domain of f,g with g(x)≠0.
(x²−4)/(x−2)=x+2 only for x≠2.

Composition
(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)) evaluates g first then f.
Output of the inner function must belong to the outer function's domain.
f(x)=x²,g(x)=x+1 implies (f∘g)(x)=(x+1)².

Composition order
In general f∘g≠g∘f.
Even when both exist, inner/outer meaning and units determine the valid order.
d(hours) gives miles and u(miles) gives gallons, so u(d(hours)).

Table and graph composition
Follow the first mapping to an intermediate value, then apply the second mapping.
A missing intermediate table input makes that composition undefined.
If g(1)=2 and f(2)=5, then f(g(1))=5.

Composite domain
The allowed x-values are in the inner domain and map to allowed inputs of the outer function.
D(f∘g)={x∈D(g):g(x)∈D(f)}.
If f(u)=1/(u−2) and g(x)=√x, exclude x<0 and x=4.

Decomposition
A complicated formula can be expressed as outer rule evaluated on inner rule.
Different valid choices for components can yield the same composite.
√(7−x²)=(u↦√u)∘(x↦7−x²).
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Different algebraic operations on functions
Let f(x)=x−2 and g(x)=x²−4. Find (g−f)(x) and (g/f)(x), including their original domains.
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: (g−f)(x)=x²−x−2 for all real x; (g/f)(x)=x+2 for x≠2.

Example 2: Composition order need not commute
For f(x)=3x+2 and g(x)=4−x, compare f(g(x)) and g(f(x)).
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: f∘g=14−3x and g∘f=2−3x, not commutative.

Example 3: Interpret a composite contextual output
Let s(t) count steps walked by time t (minutes); let c(s) be estimated kilocalories expended after s steps. Interpret c(s(5)).
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: c(s(5)) describes estimated energy expended (kilocalories) from a five-minute walk.

Example 4: Choose a meaningful function order
Let d(h) map travel hours to miles driven; let u(m) map miles driven to gallons used. Which expression predicts gallons after h hours?
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: u(d(h)) with units gallons; the reverse composition lacks the declared interface.

Example 5: Nested lookup from two tables
Let f(1)=5, f(2)=4, f(3)=1 and g(1)=3, g(2)=1, g(3)=2. Evaluate f(g(1)) and g(f(3)).
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: f(g(1))=1; g(f(3))=3.

Example 6: Composition from graph coordinates
Independent graphs show g(1)=2 and f(2)=5. Find f(g(1)), explaining how two graph readings are combined.
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: f(g(1))=5.

Example 7: Nested formula numeric evaluation
Let f(t)=t²−2t and h(x)=2x+3. Evaluate f(h(2)) and h(f(2)).
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: f(h(2))=35 and h(f(2))=3.

Example 8: Domain of nested quotient functions
Let f(x)=6/(x−2) and g(x)=3/(x−1). Find domain of f(g(x)).
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: Domain (−∞,1)∪(1,5/2)∪(5/2,∞).

Example 9: Decomposition into inner and outer maps
Write H(x)=√(7−x²) as a composition using independent functions.
Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Answer: a(x)=7−x²; b(u)=√u, with H=b(a(x)), domain [−√7,√7].
Translations.StepByStepSolutions:
1. Different algebraic operations on functions
Step 1: (g−f)(x)=x²−4−(x−2)=x²−x−2.
Step 2: (g/f)(x)=(x²−4)/(x−2)=(x+2)(x−2)/(x−2).
Step 3: Although the quotient simplifies, the original divisor vanishes at x=2.

2. Composition order need not commute
Step 1: f(g(x))=3(4−x)+2=14−3x.
Step 2: g(f(x))=4−(3x+2)=2−3x.
Step 3: The outputs differ by 12 at every x.

3. Interpret a composite contextual output
Step 1: The inner function s(5) converts five minutes into step count.
Step 2: That step count is a valid input to outer c.
Step 3: The composite output is kilocalories expended from the steps walked during the first five minutes.

4. Choose a meaningful function order
Step 1: Compute d(h) first (miles).
Step 2: Feed the result as the miles input to u.
Step 3: The reverse composition d(u(m)) treats gallons as hours and is physically mismatched.

5. Nested lookup from two tables
Step 1: g(1)=3, so f(g(1))=f(3)=1.
Step 2: f(3)=1, so g(f(3))=g(1)=3.
Step 3: Every intermediate value must be in the input domain of the next table.

6. Composition from graph coordinates
Step 1: Start on the g graph at x=1 to obtain output 2.
Step 2: Use 2 as the x-input on the f graph and read output 5.
Step 3: Validate: Read actual plotted coordinates, not the original input twice.

7. Nested formula numeric evaluation
Step 1: h(2)=7 and f(7)=49−14=35.
Step 2: f(2)=4−4=0 and h(0)=3.
Step 3: Validate: The inner function must be evaluated before the outer function.

8. Domain of nested quotient functions
Step 1: Inner denominator excludes x=1.
Step 2: Outer denominator excludes input g(x)=2.
Step 3: 3/(x−1)=2 implies x=5/2; exclude this additional input.

9. Decomposition into inner and outer maps
Step 1: Define inside a(x)=7−x².
Step 2: Define outside b(u)=√u for u≥0.
Step 3: Then H=b∘a and its real domain requires 7−x²≥0.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Applying the outer function before the inner function.
Why: Composition f(g(x)) is nested evaluation and order matters.
Correction: Evaluate g(x) first then feed its result to f.

Restoring a cancelled denominator zero to the quotient domain.
Why: The original division remains undefined.
Correction: Track exclusions from the unsimplified quotient.

Checking the domain of only the inner function.
Why: The output may be forbidden by the outer function.
Correction: Intersect the inner domain with g(x)∈D(f).

Assuming the two composition orders always agree.
Why: Composition is generally not commutative.
Correction: Evaluate both orders and check their units and domains.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Arithmetic on functions is pointwise and division excludes denominator zeros.

2. (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)) applies the inner function first; changing order may change meaning.

3. For table/graph composition each intermediate output must be a valid next input.

4. A composite domain restricts both the inner rule and the outer rule's accepted inputs.

5. Contextual unit compatibility helps identify meaningful composition order.

6. First-party open-ended source skills are teacher-reviewed in Stage C.

Translations.Title: Transformation of Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: shift graphs vertically and horizontally, reflect about axes, identify even/odd symmetry, stretch/compress inputs and outputs, and combine several transformations while tracking original domain restrictions.

For g(x)=f(x)+k output values shift up or down by k. For g(x)=f(x−h), graph moves right h despite the subtraction inside.

For −f(x), negate the output, reflecting across horizontal x-axis. For f(−x), negate each input to reflect across the vertical y-axis. An even function is unchanged under f(−x); an odd function changes to −f(x).

Multiplying outputs g(x)=a f(x) gives vertical scaling; multiplying inputs g(x)=f(bx) changes horizontal scaling inversely. Negative factors may add reflection.

A contextual formula's units reveal whether the change is to an input or to an output. Never add miles directly to dollars or years directly to population.

For combined transformations apply the input substitution and output scaling carefully, then check vertex/endpoints, asymptotes and domain.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) For f(x)=|x| give the vertex and range of g(x)=2f(x−3)−4. (b) For h(x)=√x explain the domain of h(−x). (c) Determine if p(x)=x³−5x is odd, even, or neither.

Independent Try It 1 — Model vertical shift. A ball's height is h(t)=−5t²+30t metres. Write new height b(t) if launched 8 m above ground.

Independent Try It 2 — Root horizontal shift. For f(x)=√x, graph g(x)=f(x+2). Give new startpoint and domain.

Independent Try It 3 — Absolute-value translation. For f(x)=|x|, graph h(x)=f(x−3)+2. Identify its vertex.

Independent Try It 4 — Reciprocal combined shift. Transform y=1/x one unit right and one up.

Independent Try It 5 — Reflect an absolute value graph. Reflect f(x)=|x−1| about x-axis and about y-axis separately.

Independent Try It 6 — Reflect finite table. If f(−1)=5,f(0)=8,f(2)=3, create tables for −f(x) and f(−x).

Independent Try It 7 — Reflect an even function. Given f(x)=x², find −f(x) and f(−x). Explain difference.

Independent Try It 8 — Even or odd polynomial. Classify f(x)=x⁴+2x²+5.

Independent Try It 9 — Compress vertical table. Given f(1)=8, f(2)=12, f(3)=16, find g(x)=(3/4)f(x).

Independent Try It 10 — Stretch and translate identity. Vertically stretch f(x)=x by 3 and then shift down 2.

Independent Try It 11 — Stretch square root horizontally. Construct √x stretched horizontally by 3.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Vertical shifts
g(x)=f(x)+k moves a graph vertically by k output units.
Domain unchanged; range shifts by k.
x²+3 has vertex (0,3).

Horizontal shifts
g(x)=f(x−h) shifts right h; f(x+h) shifts left h.
Input changes have opposite sign to visual displacement.
|x−2| vertex (2,0).

Reflections
−f(x) reflects across x-axis; f(−x) reflects across y-axis.
Negating output differs from negating input.
−√x has nonpositive range, √(−x) has nonpositive domain.

Even/odd parity
Even means f(−x)=f(x); odd means f(−x)=−f(x).
Verify domain symmetry and algebra; many functions are neither.
x² is even, x³ is odd, (x−1)² neither.

Vertical scale
g(x)=a·f(x) stretches for |a|>1 and compresses for 0<|a|<1.
Negative a also reflects vertically.
2x² doubles outputs.

Horizontal scale
g(x)=f(bx) compresses horizontally if |b|>1 and stretches if 0<|b|<1.
Compare input coordinates using x_new=x_old/b.
f(3x) shifts old features x=6 to x=2.

Combined transformations
Apply inside input changes, then output changes; factor inner affine term to locate horizontal shift.
Transform endpoints and preserve allowed-domain preimages.
f((x+2)/2)−3 shifts stretched graph left 2 and down 3.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Vertical translation in a context
A rooftop sensor records open area A(t) square metres; its redesigned value is always 3 m² higher. Express the transformation.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: A_new(t)=A(t)+3; each plotted y-coordinate increases by 3 while time stays fixed.

Example 2: Translate a table vertically
For x=[0,2,4,6] and f(x)=[2,5,7,9], construct g(x)=f(x)−2.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g outputs [0,3,5,7], with inputs unchanged.

Example 3: Shift a schedule earlier
A shift schedule is represented by S(t). The plan begins one hour earlier without altering the output sequence. Define shifted function.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: T(t)=S(t+1), a horizontal shift left one hour.

Example 4: Translate a table horizontally
For f(1)=3,f(3)=5,f(5)=7, tabulate g(x)=f(x−2) at the appropriate new inputs.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g(3)=3,g(5)=5,g(7)=7; every x-value shifts right 2.

Example 5: Identify a shifted parabola
An upward parabola has the same shape as y=x² but a vertex at (−3,0). Find its rule.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g(x)=(x+3)²; horizontal shift left 3.

Example 6: Compare input versus output shifts in context
For a distance-to-cost function C(m) dollars for m miles, interpret C(m)+5 and C(m+5).
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: The first adds a $5 fee; the second prices five extra miles.

Example 7: Combine horizontal and vertical shifts
Transform f(x)=|x| into h(x)=f(x−2)+3; state vertex and range.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: h(x)=|x−2|+3 with vertex (2,3), domain ℝ and range [3,∞).

Example 8: Recover a shifted root function
A square-root curve begins at (−2,4) and retains the toolkit shape. Give its rule and domain/range.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g(x)=√(x+2)+4; domain [−2,∞), range [4,∞).

Example 9: Reflect a square-root graph
Reflect f(x)=√x in each coordinate axis separately.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: Across x-axis: −√x with domain x≥0; across y-axis: √(−x) with domain x≤0.

Example 10: Reflect a finite mapping
f(1)=2,f(3)=5,f(4)=7. Give −f(x) and f(−x) tabulations.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: −f: (1,−2),(3,−5),(4,−7); f(−x): (−1,2),(−3,5),(−4,7).

Example 11: Combine reflection and translation
Transform y=2^x into k(x)=1−2^(−x); identify reflection and shift.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: Reflect horizontally y=2^(−x), then vertically −2^(−x), then up 1; range (−∞,1).

Example 12: Test odd and even algebraically
Classify f(x)=x³+4x.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: Odd, since f(−x)=−x³−4x=−f(x); origin symmetry.

Example 13: Vertical scaling in a measured context
A city's weekly count is P(t). A new city follows twice the output at each corresponding week. Express graph relation.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: Q(t)=2P(t), vertical stretch factor 2.

Example 14: Vertical compression of a table
Given f(1)=4,f(2)=10,f(3)=12, form g(x)=(1/2)f(x).
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g(1)=2,g(2)=5,g(3)=6.

Example 15: Identify vertical stretch in a cubic
A transformed cubic passes through (1,3), (0,0), (−1,−3) and is g(x)=a·x³. Determine a.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: a=3, so g(x)=3x³; vertical stretch factor 3.

Example 16: Horizontal compression of a time series
An activity model Q(t) follows the original profile P but evolves three times as quickly. Write transformation.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: Q(t)=P(3t); each original event at t=a occurs at t=a/3.

Example 17: Horizontal stretch of a table
For f(2)=3,f(4)=5,f(6)=7, create g(x)=f(x/2) at known inputs.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g(4)=3,g(8)=5,g(12)=7; x doubles for matching outputs.

Example 18: Identify horizontal compression from coordinate pairs
The original graph contains a feature (6,4) and transformed graph has feature (2,4) with unchanged height. State scaling.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g(x)=f(3x), horizontal compression by factor 1/3.

Example 19: Transform a table in three steps
For f(3)=5,f(6)=8,f(9)=10, tabulate g(x)=2f(3x)+1.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: g(1)=11,g(2)=17,g(3)=21.

Example 20: Compose three graph transformations
For f(x)=|x|, give k(x)=f((x+2)/2)−3 and identify each transformation.
Method: Use first-party input/output transformation rules, preserve units, and verify domain and marked graph points.
Answer: k(x)=|(x+2)/2|−3=(1/2)|x+2|−3; vertex (−2,−3), range [−3,∞).

Translations.CommonMistakes:
Moving a graph left for f(x−3).
Why: Input−3 is matched at x three units larger.
Correction: Shift f(x−3) right three.

Treating f(−x) as −f(x).
Why: Horizontal and vertical reflections affect different coordinates.
Correction: Use f(−x) for y-axis reflection, −f(x) for x-axis reflection.

Treating f(3x) as a threefold horizontal stretch.
Why: The input attains prior values at one-third its previous x.
Correction: The horizontal length scale becomes 1/3.

Classifying a function as even/odd without symmetric domain.
Why: f(−x) must be defined whenever f(x) is.
Correction: Verify both domain symmetry and parity identity.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Output shifts f(x)+k move the graph vertically by k.

2. Input shifts f(x−h) move graph horizontally right h.

3. −f(x) reflects outputs; f(−x) reflects input coordinates.

4. Even functions satisfy f(−x)=f(x), odd functions satisfy f(−x)=−f(x).

5. Outside multiplication scales vertically; inside multiplication scales inversely horizontally.

6. Preserve valid original domain restrictions under every transformation.

Translations.Title: Absolute Value Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: express numerical distances and contextual tolerances with |x−a|, construct transformed absolute-value graphs, solve absolute equations and graph absolute inequalities.

The absolute value |x−a| is a nonnegative distance. For a nonnegative tolerance d, |x−a|≤d includes all x from a−d through a+d, while |x−a|≥d describes two external rays.

The graph f(x)=a|x−h|+k has vertex (h,k). If a>0 it opens upward and attains minimum k; if a<0 it opens downward and attains maximum k.

For |A|=c: if c>0 solve A=±c; if c=0 solve A=0; if c<0 there are no real solutions. Check each candidate in the original formula.

A strict inside inequality |A|<c has two simultaneous bounds; an outside inequality |A|>c describes separate rays. When multiplying or dividing inequalities by a negative factor, reverse the sign.

Graph intercepts require setting the appropriate coordinate to zero. Always state endpoints and included/excluded bounds for real-domain and graph window problems.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) Solve |x+2|≤4 using interval notation. (b) For f(x)=−2|x−3|+4 state vertex, range and x-intercepts. (c) Explain why |3x−1|=−2 has no solution.

Independent Try It 1 — Distance from center. Find all x within two units of −1.

Independent Try It 2 — Test passing score. A score within 15 points of 75 meets a stated requirement. Express inclusive absolute-value inequality.

Independent Try It 3 — Graph a V transformation. Reflect f(x)=|x| over x-axis, then shift right 2 and up 4.

Independent Try It 4 — Solve for both roots. Find zeros of f(x)=|2x+3|−5.

Independent Try It 5 — Locate graph intercepts. Find intercepts of f(x)=−|x+1|+4.

Independent Try It 6 — Inclusive absolute inequality. Solve |x−3|≤5.

Independent Try It 7 — Inequality after dividing by negative. Solve −2|k−4|≤−6.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Absolute distance
|x−a| denotes nonnegative real distance of x from a.
|x−a|≤d for d≥0 is the closed interval [a−d,a+d].
|x−6|≤3 gives [3,9].

Absolute V-shape
f(x)=a|x−h|+k has corner/vertex (h,k).
Sign of a controls opening, |a| controls steepness; domain all real.
−2|x+1|+4 opens down from (−1,4).

Absolute equations
If |A|=c with c>0, then A=c or A=−c.
For c<0 there are no solutions; for c=0 solve A=0.
|2x−3|=5 gives x=4 or −1.

Absolute inequalities
Inside ≤ yields intersection; outside ≥ yields two rays for a nonnegative bound.
For negative bounds examine the nonnegative absolute value before case splitting.
|x−3|≤5 gives [−2,8]; |x−3|>5 gives two rays.

Intercepts
Set y=0 for x-intercepts and x=0 for y-intercept.
An upward shifted V may have no x-intercepts even though it always has a y-intercept.
2|x−1|+3 has no x-intercepts.

Context and units
Engineering tolerances model bounded deviations.
State center, allowable distance, inclusion, units and interpretation.
|R−10000|≤200 Ω.

Viewing windows
A bounded plotted x-window generally has a range different from the full real-domain range.
Check vertex inside the window and both included endpoints.
10|x−2| on [0,4] attains [0,20].
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Model a symmetric number-line tolerance
Find all real numbers within or exactly three units of six.
Method: Use nonnegative absolute-distance definitions, source-skill V-graph properties, exact algebraic intervals and teacher review.
Answer: |x−6|≤3, so x∈[3,9].

Example 2: Manufacturing tolerance with units
A resistor rated at 10 kΩ allows a ±2% tolerance. Express acceptable resistance R in ohms and interval notation.
Method: Use nonnegative absolute-distance definitions, source-skill V-graph properties, exact algebraic intervals and teacher review.
Answer: |R−10000|≤200 ohms; R∈[9800,10200] ohms.

Example 3: Recover the V-shape equation
An upward V-shaped graph has vertex (−1,−3) and crosses the vertical axis at (0,−1). Determine f(x)=a|x−h|+k.
Method: Use nonnegative absolute-distance definitions, source-skill V-graph properties, exact algebraic intervals and teacher review.
Answer: f(x)=2|x+1|−3, with a=2, vertex (−1,−3), range [−3,∞).

Example 4: Compute zeros of an absolute-value function
Find all zeros of f(x)=|3x+2|−8.
Method: Use nonnegative absolute-distance definitions, source-skill V-graph properties, exact algebraic intervals and teacher review.
Answer: 3x+2=±8; x=2 or x=−10/3.

Example 5: Recognize a no-solution equation
Solve 2|x−1|+3=1.
Method: Use nonnegative absolute-distance definitions, source-skill V-graph properties, exact algebraic intervals and teacher review.
Answer: No real solution: a nonnegative absolute term cannot yield −2.

Example 6: Solve a strict absolute inequality
Solve |x−4|<3.
Method: Use nonnegative absolute-distance definitions, source-skill V-graph properties, exact algebraic intervals and teacher review.
Answer: −3<x−4<3, so x∈(1,7).

Example 7: Solve where a transformed V graph is below zero
For f(x)=−(1/2)|2x−5|+3, find all x with f(x)<0.
Method: Use nonnegative absolute-distance definitions, source-skill V-graph properties, exact algebraic intervals and teacher review.
Answer: |2x−5|>6, so x<−1/2 or x>11/2.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions:
1. Model a symmetric number-line tolerance

Translations.CommonMistakes:
Splitting |A|=−2 into two equations.
Why: Absolute values cannot be negative.
Correction: Conclude no real solutions before splitting.

Writing an OR statement for |x−a|<d.
Why: Inside a radius imposes simultaneous lower and upper bounds.
Correction: Use a−d<x<a+d for d>0.

Neglecting to reverse inequality when dividing by a negative multiplier.
Why: This reverses which real values satisfy the inequality.
Correction: Reverse the comparison direction on negative division.

Confusing the vertex location with graph intercepts.
Why: Vertex generally has nonzero x or y coordinate.
Correction: Set x=0/y=0 explicitly to find intercepts.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Absolute value represents nonnegative distance from a target.

2. V-shaped functions have a vertex determined by horizontal and vertical shifts.

3. An equation |A|=c has no real solution if c<0.

4. Inside inequalities produce bounded intervals; outside inequalities usually produce two rays.

5. Always check boundary inclusions, intercepts, graph window and physical units.

6. Teacher reviews diagrams and source-skill reasoning in Stage C.

Translations.Title: Inverse Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: identify one-to-one functions, invert table and graph coordinates, test inverse pairs by composition, compute inverse algebraically, and correctly exchange domain/range including physical units.

If f(a)=b for one-to-one f, the inverse satisfies f⁻¹(b)=a. The inverse must be a function, so f must pass the horizontal-line test on its chosen domain.

Graph f and f⁻¹ are symmetric across y=x: every original point (a,b) corresponds to an inverse point (b,a). Inverse is not the same as reciprocal 1/f.

Algebraic inversion solves y=f(x) for the input variable, swaps symbols, and preserves exclusions and necessary branch restrictions. Verify both compositions when possible.

An unrestricted quadratic or absolute-value function is not one-to-one. Restrict to a monotonic branch before claiming a functional inverse.

The inverse domain equals the original range, and the inverse range equals the original domain. Physical models swap output/input units.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) Find inverse of f(x)=2x−6 and verify by composition. (b) Explain why f(x)=x² requires an injective domain restriction. (c) For g(x)=4+√(x−1), determine inverse formula and its domain.

Independent Try It 1 — Swap a given inverse pair. If h⁻¹(7)=3, what exact original mapping must h contain?

Independent Try It 2 — Test inverse cubic translation. For f(x)=x³−4 and g(x)=∛(x+4), verify both compositions.

Independent Try It 3 — Cube translated inverse. For f(x)=(x−1)³, is g(x)=∛x+1 an inverse?

Independent Try It 4 — Swap domain and range. A one-to-one f has domain (1,∞) and range (−∞,−2). Give inverse domain and range.

Independent Try It 5 — Invert finite table. For a one-to-one table f(1)=5,f(2)=7,f(3)=9, evaluate f⁻¹(7).

Independent Try It 6 — Graph inverse coordinate lookup. For a source-skill graph model g(x)=x+3, read g(2) and g⁻¹(2).

Independent Try It 7 — Solve formula for input. Solve y=(x−5)/3 for x in terms of y.

Independent Try It 8 — Inverse of a decreasing root. For f(x)=2−√x, x≥0, derive its inverse and state its allowable domain.

Independent Try It 9 — Graph a function and its rational inverse. Reflect points from f(x)=3/(x−2)+5 across y=x. Derive inverse formula.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Inverse function
If f(a)=b for a one-to-one function then f⁻¹(b)=a.
Swap input/output roles and original domain/range.
f(2)=7 ↔ f⁻¹(7)=2.

One-to-one and horizontal line test
Inverse of a function is a function only when each original output has at most one input.
A horizontal line may intersect the graph no more than once.
Unrestricted y=x² fails the horizontal line test.

Composition proof
For inverse pair f,g both f∘g and g∘f act as identity on their corresponding valid domains.
Do not forget exclusions where an inner rule is undefined.
f(x)=1/(x+3),g(x)=1/x−3.

Algebraic inversion
Write y=f(x), solve for x in terms of y, exchange variables and preserve restrictions.
Some formulas require selecting an injective branch.
f(x)=3+√(x−2) invertible with inverse (x−3)²+2 on x≥3.

Domain and range interchange
Domain of f⁻¹ equals range of f and range of f⁻¹ equals domain of f.
Swapping without checking endpoints yields incorrect domains.
√x on [0,∞) has inverse x² restricted x≥0.

Graph symmetry
An inverse graph is the reflection of f across the identity line y=x.
Each point (a,b) maps to (b,a).
(3,5) in f becomes (5,3) in f⁻¹.

Units in inverse models
An inverse changes dependent output back into the input quantity.
Units of original output become inverse input units.
Distance in miles ↔ time in minutes.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Reverse an input-output mapping
A one-to-one mapping has f(2)=7 and f(5)=12. Find the matching inverse values.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: f⁻¹(7)=2; f⁻¹(12)=5.

Example 2: Prove an inverse by composing in both orders
Given f(x)=1/(x+3) and g(x)=1/x−3, determine if they are inverse functions including their proper domains.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: f(g(x))=x for x≠0; g(f(x))=x for x≠−3. Yes, they are inverse functions.

Example 3: Distinguish a multiplier from a fractional exponent
Is g(x)=x/3 the inverse of f(x)=x³?
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: No. f(g(x))=x³/27. Correct inverse is g(x)=∛x.

Example 4: Restrict domain before inverting a noninjective family
Explain how to make x², |x| and 1/x² invertible by an admissible branch restriction.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: For f(x)=x² choose x≥0 and inverse √x. For |x| choose x≥0; for 1/x² choose x>0 yielding 1/√y for y>0.

Example 5: Interpret a tabulated inverse
A trip log gives f(20)=12 miles, f(40)=25 miles and f(60)=50 miles, with input minutes. Interpret f⁻¹(50).
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: f⁻¹(50)=60 minutes; the 50-mile reading occurs after 60 minutes.

Example 6: Read a graph and its inverse
An independently plotted one-to-one linear model is g(x)=x−1. Find g(3) and g⁻¹(3) from points.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: g(3)=2, g⁻¹(3)=4; the input/output roles are reversed.

Example 7: Invert Fahrenheit and Celsius units
Given C=(5/9)(F−32), express Fahrenheit F in terms of Celsius C.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: F=(9/5)C+32.

Example 8: Inverse of a shifted rational rule
For f(x)=3/(x−2)+5, solve for f⁻¹(x) and state both input domains.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: f⁻¹(x)=3/(x−5)+2; original x≠2; inverse x≠5.

Example 9: Inverse of a shifted square root
For f(x)=3+√(x−2), find inverse rule, domain and range.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: f⁻¹(x)=(x−3)²+2 for x≥3; original domain [2,∞), range [3,∞).

Example 10: Plot the reflected inverse across y=x
For f(x)=x+2 and f⁻¹(x)=x−2, plot three points from each and explain the symmetry.
Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Answer: Source points (−1,1),(0,2),(2,4) reflect to inverse points (1,−1),(2,0),(4,2) across y=x.

2. Prove an inverse by composing in both orders

Step 2: f(g(x))=x for x≠0; g(f(x))=x for x≠−3. Yes, they are inverse functions.
Step 3: Validate: Respect the distinct input restrictions.

3. Distinguish a multiplier from a fractional exponent

Step 1: Plan: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Step 2: For f(x)=x² choose x≥0 and inverse √x. For |x| choose x≥0; for 1/x² choose x>0 yielding 1/√y for y>0.

5. Interpret a tabulated inverse

Step 3: Validate: Inverse inputs carry miles, inverse outputs minutes.

6. Read a graph and its inverse
Step 1: Plan: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
