Step 3: Validate: g(4)=3 confirms the inverse read.

7. Invert Fahrenheit and Celsius units
Step 1: Plan: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Step 2: F=(9/5)C+32.
Step 3: Validate: Recomposing with C(F) returns the starting temperature.

8. Inverse of a shifted rational rule
Step 1: Plan: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Step 2: f⁻¹(x)=3/(x−5)+2; original x≠2; inverse x≠5.
Step 3: Validate: Check both compositions on their allowed domains.

9. Inverse of a shifted square root
Step 1: Plan: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Step 2: f⁻¹(x)=(x−3)²+2 for x≥3; original domain [2,∞), range [3,∞).
Step 3: Validate: The inverse quadratic is restricted to x≥3.

10. Plot the reflected inverse across y=x
Step 1: Plan: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Step 2: Source points (−1,1),(0,2),(2,4) reflect to inverse points (1,−1),(2,0),(4,2) across y=x.
Step 3: Validate: Reflected inverse swaps domain and range.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Writing f⁻¹(x)=1/f(x).
Why: Inverse functions reverse inputs/outputs; reciprocals divide 1 by output.
Correction: Solve y=f(x) for x and swap variables.

Inverting x² on ℝ without restricting input sign.
Why: Two distinct inputs can produce one output.
Correction: Choose x≥0 or x≤0 before finding a functional inverse.

Forgetting inverse domain restrictions after squaring a radical equation.
Why: The new quadratic formula may allow outputs the original root never attained.
Correction: Use original range as inverse domain.

Reading g⁻¹(3) by finding g(3).
Why: The inverse question asks for an input whose original output is 3.
Correction: Read the original graph at y=3 then return its x-coordinate.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. One-to-one functions pass the horizontal-line test.

2. An inverse reverses inputs and outputs; it is not the reciprocal function.

3. Composition with an inverse returns the identity on the appropriate domain.

4. An inverse graph is the reflection of the original graph in y=x.

5. Restrictions and included endpoints swap when domains and ranges exchange.

6. Teacher evaluates independent source-skill graph inversions manually in Stage C.

Translations.Title: Linear Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Original learning aims: identify and interpret linear models f(x)=mx+b, determine whether behavior increases/decreases/is constant, calculate rate from points, write slope-intercept and point-slope equations, and model tables/contexts.

Slope is a constant rate (change in output)/(change in input). The sign determines increasing or decreasing behavior. A line has slope m and initial value b=f(0).

Given a point and slope, use y−y1=m(x−x1). Given two points, first compute m, then solve for b.

An actual model should state units, physical domain and the meaning of its initial value. Tables require a constant rate on every pair of neighboring measurements.

Independent Edulytics cool-down: (a) Find f(x)=mx+b through (−1,2) and (3,10). (b) What do slope and intercept mean in C(n)=150+8n? (c) Decide if x=5 represents y as a function of x.

Independent Try It 1 — Identify slope and initial value. For f(t)=8t+15, state initial value, rate, and behavior.

Independent Try It 2 — Classify by slope. Classify f(x)=−3x+7, g(x)=0x+5 and h(x)=2x−1.

Independent Try It 3 — Two-point slope. Compute slope through (−2,4),(2,10).

Independent Try It 4 — Point-slope equation. Find line slope 4 through (2,−3).

Independent Try It 5 — Cost from fixed charge. With initial charge $40 and $12 per item, write C(n) and compute C(5).

Independent Try It 6 — Table linearity. A table x=0,2,4,6 has outputs 3,7,11,15. Find f.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Linear equation
A linear function has form f(x)=mx+b with a constant rate.
Slope m describes output change per input; b=f(0).
f(x)=2x+3.

Slope from coordinates
m=(y2−y1)/(x2−x1) for distinct inputs.
Both coordinate differences must follow matching endpoint order.
From (1,3) to (3,7), m=2.

Increasing/decreasing
Sign of m controls monotonicity.
Positive slopes increase, negatives decrease; zero slope is constant.
−4x+3 decreases.

Point-slope form
A line through (x1,y1) with slope m satisfies y−y1=m(x−x1).
Convert to y=mx+b by expanding.
y−2=3(x−1).

Intercepts
b=f(0), while x-intercept solves mx+b=0.
For m≠0, x-intercept is −b/m.
2x+6 intercept at x=−3.

Linear model units
Each unit increase in x changes output by m output units.
State physical domain, units and initial value.
C(n)=900+25n for nonnegative item counts.

Linear table test
Successive data pairs lie on one line iff all pairwise slopes match.
Use Δy/Δx even for unequal input gaps.
x=0,2,4; f=1,5,9.

Vertical and horizontal lines
A vertical line x=c is not a function y=f(x) on a multi-y graph.
A horizontal line y=c is a constant function.
x=2 is vertical.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Interpret linear depth model
A sensor reports pressure P(d)=0.45d+15 (psi), where d is depth in feet. Interpret its initial value and slope.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: P(0)=15 psi; pressure increases by 0.45 psi per foot.

Example 2: Increasing/decreasing/constant models
Compare number-of-items models A(t)=45t, B(t)=240−12t and C(t)=18. Classify their monotonicity.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: Increasing A; decreasing B; constant C.

Example 3: Slope between two points
Find slope of the line through (2,−1) and (7,3), and describe direction.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: m=(3−(−1))/(7−2)=4/5, increasing.

Example 4: Rate from dated population samples
Population changes from 14,200 in 2018 to 16,600 in 2022. Assume a linear model and give annual slope.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: (16600−14200)/(2022−2018)=600 people/year.

Example 5: Point-slope to slope-intercept
Write a line with slope 2 passing through (5,−1).
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: y+1=2(x−5); y=2x−11.

Example 6: Line through two points
Find a line through (2,3),(6,11) in point-slope and slope-intercept forms.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: m=2; y−3=2(x−2), y=2x−1.

Example 7: Read a line from graphed intercepts
A first-party plotted line contains (0,4) and (−2,−2). Find its function.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: slope 3, f(x)=3x+4.

Example 8: Constant cost and per-item cost
A small workshop pays $900 fixed rent and $25 per item. Express C(n) and say what slope represents.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: C(n)=900+25n dollars, n≥0 items; slope $25/item.

Example 9: Solve two plotted values for a linear rule
Suppose f(2)=−1 and f(7)=9 for a linear f. Find a slope-intercept equation.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: m=2; f(x)=2x−5.

Example 10: Total from initial count and monthly additions
A library begins with 300 recordings and adds 12 monthly. Find N(t) and N(12).
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: N(t)=300+12t, N(12)=444.

Example 11: Infer base fee and commission from two invoices
An employee is paid $680 for four sales and $840 for eight sales. Find base plus per-sale commission.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: slope $40/sale; base $520; I(n)=520+40n.

Example 12: Convert a table to one linear function
A recorded sequence has weeks w=0,2,4,6 and values 900,960,1020,1080. Find model.
Method: Compute slope/intercept or apply the linear function skill with units.
Answer: P(w)=900+30w; uniform rate 30/week.

Why: Units and slope are inverted.

4. Two distinct points determine one line.

5. Modeling requires appropriate units and admissible domains.

Translations.Title: Graphs of Linear Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: graph lines by plotting points and using slope/intercepts; infer a line formula from a graph; identify parallel and perpendicular relationships; construct lines through points; solve two-line systems.

To graph f(x)=mx+b, mark (0,b), then move horizontally and vertically according to rise/run. Check a second point for accuracy.

Two distinct nonvertical lines are parallel iff they have equal slope. Perpendicular nonzero slopes multiply to −1. A vertical line x=c is perpendicular to a horizontal y=k.

Find line formulas from two coordinates or from an intercept and slope. A vertical line cannot be expressed as a single-valued y=f(x) over its x-coordinate.

The intersection of two lines has the same x-input and y-output for both equations. Algebraically solve f(x)=g(x) and substitute back.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) Sketch y=−2x+4 from its intercept and rise/run. (b) Find a perpendicular through (1,2) to y=2x−3. (c) Solve intersection of y=x+1 and y=5−x.

Independent Try It 1 — Graph by coordinates. Plot f(x)=−3x/4+6 using x=0,4,8.

Independent Try It 2 — Find negative-input point. For f(x)=−2x/3+5 find a point with negative x.

Independent Try It 3 — Transform a line. Describe identity transformations producing y=2x+4.

Independent Try It 4 — Find zero. Find x-intercept of y=x/4−4.

Independent Try It 5 — Parallel and perpendicular through origin. Given h(x)=2x−4, find a parallel line through origin and a perpendicular one.

Independent Try It 6 — Perpendicular to two-point line. Line through (−2,−15),(2,−3): find a perpendicular through (6,4).

Independent Try It 7 — Analyze two intersecting models. For j(t)=3t−4, h(t)=5−t: find each intercept, slope signs and intersection.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Graphing by points
Substitute 2 or more x-coordinates into a linear function.
Three points provide a useful error check.
f(x)=x+1 goes through (0,1),(1,2).

Slope-intercept graph
Plot b at (0,b) then use slope m as rise/run.
A negative slope lowers y as x increases.
m=−2/3 descends2 for 3 right.

Line from graph
Read any two distinct plotted points to find slope, then solve intercept.
Avoid reading noisy grid labels without point confirmation.
(0,4),(2,8) yields y=2x+4.

Special lines
y=k is horizontal and constant; x=k is vertical and not a function y=f(x).
Horizontal slope0; vertical undefined.
x=3 fails vertical line test.

Parallel relationships
Distinct nonvertical lines are parallel when their slopes coincide.
Distinct y-intercepts distinguish parallel lines.
2x+1 and 2x−3.

Perpendicular relationships
Nonvertical/nonhorizontal perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
Vertical is perpendicular to horizontal.
m=3 and m=−1/3.

Equation through point
Use y−y1=m(x−x1) with the required slope.
For a perpendicular slope take negative reciprocal.
m=4 through (2,−1) yields 4x−9.

Linear systems
At intersection the outputs of both functions are equal.
Solve f(x)=g(x) and substitute into one.
2x−3=5−x at x=8/3.

Break-even
Sales revenue equals total fixed plus variable production cost.
Check units and admissible nonnegative quantities.

Translations.Title: Modeling with Linear Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning aims: identify model inputs and outputs, translate verbal descriptions into affine equations, use diagrams for quantities and spatial measurements, and build/solve systems to compare practical choices.

The statement 'starts at b and gains m per unit' corresponds to y=mx+b. Explain the rate and initial value with units.

Two data points identify the linear slope. Check whether the resulting formula should apply only within a specific time interval or other realistic domain.

Geometric modeling may require a Pythagorean distance formula before simplification. Distances, times and cardinal directions must retain their units.

Competing plans should be compared as two functions of the same input variable. Their break-even point solves C1(x)=C2(x), but preferring one plan requires evaluating the appropriate inequality.

Independent Edulytics cool-down: (a) A supply model has $125 fixed cost and $3 per unit. Find C(40). (b) A population is 600 in year0 and 750 in year3; find P(t). (c) Compare A(d)=20+2d with B(d)=60+d and find when B saves money.

Independent Try It 1 — Model fixed and variable manufacturing cost. A workshop pays $30,000 rent and $0.40 for each item. Write cost C(n), initial value and units.

Independent Try It 2 — Forecast and threshold from a two-year trend. A town has 20,000 people in 2020 and 24,000 in 2024. Under a linear continuation find 2026 population and year of 30,000.

Independent Try It 3 — Use perpendicular projection geometry. Road segment points from town A=(0,0) to B=(30,40) km. Find travelled straight-line length to a junction at (12,16).
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Identify variables
The independent quantity is the controllable input and the dependent quantity changes with it.
Choose units and realistic nonnegative domain.
Number of items n → cost C(n).

Constant-rate model
Linear model y=mx+b when the rate Δy/Δx is constant.
Estimate m from two observed points, then determine b.
P(t)=7500+300t.

Extrapolation caveat
Forecasting a linear trend beyond observations assumes the rate stays unchanged.
An extrapolation is a model forecast, not a guaranteed fact.
P(8)=9900 assumes annual growth remains 300.

Graph and geometry model
Perpendicular displacement components can form a right triangle.
Pythagorean length may simplify to a linear time function.
East6t, north8t gives 10t.

Parallel/perpendicular route
Coordinate geometry can express route slopes and projection points.
Use dot product or right-angle geometry for perpendicular lines.
Slope3/4 has perpendicular slope −4/3.

System of linear models
Two competing cost plans meet at equal cost.
Solve C1(x)=C2(x), then compare the two sides of threshold.
$40+1.5d versus $75+0.8d break even at d=50.

Intercept and rate in context
A model's intercept is its value at input zero.
State both quantities in physical/financial units.
Rent is $30,000 even if zero items produced.

Domain/range and units
A realistic function may be limited to the duration of a measured trend.
Do not extrapolate a nonnegative population into negative numbers.
Restrict t and explain model horizon.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Extrapolate population using a linear model
A town has 7,500 people at t=0 and 8,700 at t=4 years. Assume a linear model. Find P(t) and forecast the year t=8.
Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Answer: Slope 300 residents/year; P(t)=7500+300t; P(8)=9900. Valid only if the linear trend persists.

Example 2: Model perpendicular walking paths
Two people start together; one walks east 6 km/h and another north 8 km/h. Build a function for the straight-line separation after t hours.
Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Answer: Distance d(t)=√((6t)²+(8t)²)=10t km for t≥0, a linear distance model.

Example 3: Geometric projection in a road network
A straight route to a location 40 km east and 30 km north has a total length 50 km. Find the projection of a point (16,12) on the route and its distance along the line.
Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Answer: The point lies at two-fifths of the route, so distance from start =20 km; slope 3/4 from coordinates.

Example 4: Choose between two affine service plans
Plan A charges fixed $40 and $1.50 per kilometre; plan B $75 and $0.80/km. Find the break-even travel distance and preferred plan afterward.
Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Answer: 40+1.5d=75+0.8d; d=50 km; B cheaper for d>50.

1. Extrapolate population using a linear model
Step 1: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Step 2: Slope 300 residents/year; P(t)=7500+300t; P(8)=9900. Valid only if the linear trend persists.
Step 3: Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.

2. Model perpendicular walking paths
Step 1: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Step 2: Distance d(t)=√((6t)²+(8t)²)=10t km for t≥0, a linear distance model.
Step 3: Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.

3. Geometric projection in a road network
Step 1: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Step 2: The point lies at two-fifths of the route, so distance from start =20 km; slope 3/4 from coordinates.
Step 3: Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.

4. Choose between two affine service plans
Step 1: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Step 2: 40+1.5d=75+0.8d; d=50 km; B cheaper for d>50.
Step 3: Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Assuming a trend extrapolates indefinitely.
Why: Linear models can break beyond observed conditions.
Correction: State model assumptions and plausible horizon.

Comparing two prices with different input units.
Why: Both expressions must use the same independent quantity.
Correction: Convert to one shared variable and unit.

Treating a positive break-even equality as the cheaper-plan interval.
Why: Equality alone says neither plan is cheaper.
Correction: Solve a strict inequality for preferred option.

1. Define input/output variables and units.

2. Use constant slope and intercept to build a model.

3. Confirm the chosen physical domain and extrapolation assumptions.

4. Solve C1=C2 before comparing costs.

5. A geographic diagram can reveal lengths and perpendicular relationships.

Translations.Title: Fitting Linear Models to Data
Translations.Explanation:
Learning aims: draw and interpret scatterplots, identify a reasonable line of best fit, distinguish linear versus nonlinear patterns and predict from a linear model.

A least-squares model y=mx+b minimizes the sum of squared vertical residuals; an approximate hand-drawn line is different from a mathematical regression computation.

Pearson's r ranges from −1 through +1, with sign indicating association direction and magnitude reflecting linear association strength. Correlation does not establish causation.

Interpolation predicts at an x within the observed window. Extrapolation predicts outside it and requires an explicit caution about model reliability.

Always state the data units, observed x-range, the fitted slope/intercept and whether the graph has a curved residual pattern.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: Given paired data (0,2),(1,4),(2,6),(3,8): (a) fit an exact linear rule, (b) identify r, (c) predict at x=2.5 and x=7 and classify each prediction.

Independent Try It 1 — Predict within observed x-range. A fitted line for x∈[0,4] is y=2.2x+3. Evaluate at x=2 and classify prediction.

Independent Try It 2 — Extrapolate line with model caution. For y=2.2x+3 fitted on x=0..4, predict at x=6; identify whether extrapolation.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Scatterplot
Each paired numerical observation (x,y) is plotted as one point.
Do not connect observations unless their order and process justify it.
(1,5),(2,8).

Visual best-fit line
A line that follows the pattern of a scatterplot; not necessarily a perfect match.
Predict only when the relationship appears sufficiently straight.
y≈2.2x+3.

Least-squares regression
Choose coefficients m,b minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals.
m=Σ[(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)]/Σ[(x−x̄)²]; b=ȳ−m x̄.
First-party data has m2.2,b3.

Residual
Observed output minus model-predicted output.
A pattern in residuals can indicate an inadequate linear model.
At x2: 8−7.4=0.6.

Pearson correlation
r measures direction and strength of linear association, between −1 and 1.
Large |r| means close to line, not proof of causation.
r≈0.992 strongly positive.

Interpolation
Estimating within the span of observed independent inputs.
Predictions can still be wrong even inside observed span.
Estimate at x2.5 with 0≤x≤4.

Extrapolation
Estimating beyond original independent input range.
Explicitly flag changing conditions and weaker reliability.
Predict x6 from x∈[0,4].

Nonlinear relations
Curved scatter patterns are not well described by one affine rule.
Inspect scatter and residual shape before using regression.
x² data curve instead of straight line.

Correlation sign
Positive correlation indicates y grows on average with x; negative falls.
r near 0 means weak linear relation, not necessarily no relation.
r≈−0.9 indicates strong negative trend.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Draw and interpret a scatterplot
Plot the first-party points (0,3),(1,5),(2,8),(3,9),(4,12); describe direction and whether a line makes sense.
Method: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Answer: The pattern is strongly increasing and near-linear, but not perfectly collinear.

Example 2: Fit a line by eye
Choose a plausible straight line for data (0,3),(1,5),(2,8),(3,9),(4,12), and give its slope/intercept.
Method: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Answer: A line of rough fit y≈2.2x+3; a visual estimate need not equal least squares exactly.

Example 3: Distinguish interpolation/extrapolation
Using observed x=0 through4, predict y at x=2.5 and x=7 from y≈2.2x+3.
Method: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Answer: y(2.5)≈8.5 interpolation; y(7)≈18.4 extrapolation with higher uncertainty.

Example 4: Compute least squares without library
For first-party scatter data x=0,1,2,3,4; y=3,5,8,9,12, compute least-squares line.
Method: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Answer: m=2.2,b=3.0; minimize Σ(y−mx−b)².

Example 5: Interpret Pearson correlation
For the same five points compute r and interpret it.
Method: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Answer: Pearson r≈0.992; positive, close to one; correlation does not prove causation.

Example 6: Predict under the fitted model
Using least-squares y≈2.2x+3, estimate x=6 and state whether within observed window.
Method: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Answer: y(6)=16.2; x6 exceeds observed [0,4], so extrapolation requiring domain caveat.

Step 3: Validate: Compare fitted model to observed points and inspect extrapolation risk.

Step 2: y(2.5)≈8.5 interpolation; y(7)≈18.4 extrapolation with higher uncertainty.
Step 3: Validate: Compare fitted model to observed points and inspect extrapolation risk.

Step 3: Validate: Compare fitted model to observed points and inspect extrapolation risk.

Step 1: Plan: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Step 2: Pearson r≈0.992; positive, close to one; correlation does not prove causation.
Step 3: Validate: Compare fitted model to observed points and inspect extrapolation risk.

6. Predict under the fitted model
Step 1: Plan: Make paired-coordinate scatter observations; compute regression and correlation when appropriate.
Step 2: y(6)=16.2; x6 exceeds observed [0,4], so extrapolation requiring domain caveat.
Step 3: Validate: Compare fitted model to observed points and inspect extrapolation risk.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Assuming an r near one means the slope must be one.
Why: Correlation is unitless; slope is output/input units.
Correction: Compute slope and r separately.

Claiming correlation proves causal influence.
Why: A third variable or coincidence can create association.
Correction: Describe association without causal claim.

Treating long-distance extrapolation as confirmed fact.
Why: The observed relationship may break outside the sampled range.
Correction: State data window, forecast assumptions and caution.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Plot observations as paired points.

2. Determine whether linear fit is sensible.

3. Least squares minimizes vertical squared residuals.

4. Correlation sign and magnitude describe linear association, not causation.

5. Explicitly label interpolation vs extrapolation.

Translations.Title: Complex Numbers
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: write square roots of negative reals in terms of i, plot complex coordinates, add/subtract and multiply/divide complex numbers.

The imaginary unit i satisfies i²=−1. A complex number is a+bi with independently real and imaginary coefficients.

Complex numbers form ordered-coordinate points (real,imaginary) in the plane. Addition is component-wise and subtraction reverses each component of the subtrahend.

Multiply using distribution and i²=−1. For a quotient, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of a nonzero complex denominator.

The powers of i cycle every four. To evaluate complex-valued functions, substitute and simplify algebraically, checking that original rational denominators are not zero.

Independent Edulytics cool-down: (a) Plot z=−3+2i. (b) Compute (2−i)(3+2i). (c) Simplify (3+i)/(1−i). (d) Find i^26.

Independent Try It 1 — Negative-root conversion. Simplify √(−48).

Independent Try It 2 — Complex coordinate plotting. Plot 4−5i on complex axes.

Independent Try It 3 — Complex subtraction. Find (5+2i)−(3−4i).

Independent Try It 4 — Multiply real and complex. Find −2(3+5i).

Independent Try It 5 — Multiply two complex numbers. Find (3−2i)(1+4i).

Independent Try It 6 — Polynomial substitution. Evaluate f(z)=z²−z at z=3−i.

Independent Try It 7 — Rational substitution. Evaluate (z+1)/(z−2) at z=i.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Imaginary unit
i is defined by i²=−1.
For real a>0, √(−a)=i√a.
√−9=3i.

Complex standard form
z=a+bi with a,b real.
Re(z)=a, Im(z)=b.
2−3i has Re2, Im−3.

Complex plane
Plot (a,b) for complex a+bi.
Horizontal axis real; vertical axis imaginary.
−2+3i→(−2,3).

Addition/subtraction
Combine real parts and imaginary parts separately.
(a+bi)+(c+di)=(a+c)+(b+d)i.
(1+i)+(2−3i)=3−2i.

Complex multiplication
Distribute and replace i² by −1.
(a+bi)(c+di)=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i.
(1+i)(1−i)=2.

Conjugate
Conjugate of a+bi is a−bi.
z·conj(z)=a²+b².
Conjugate 2−i is 2+i.

Complex quotient
Multiply numerator and denominator by denominator conjugate.
A nonzero complex denominator gives a positive real a²+b².
(1+i)/(1−i)=i.

Powers of i
Powers repeat every four.
i^n is 1,i,−1,−i for n mod4=0,1,2,3.
i^37=i.

Complex substitution
Polynomial/rational functions may accept complex inputs if denominators are nonzero.
Use complex multiplication and conjugates to simplify.
(2+i)²=3+4i.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Simplify a negative square root
Write √(−25) as a complex number a+bi.
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: 5i, because i²=−1.

Example 2: Plot complex coordinate
Represent −2+3i in the Argand plane.
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: Point (−2,3), with real axis horizontal and imaginary axis vertical.

Example 3: Add two complex numbers
Compute (4−3i)+(2+5i).
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: 6+2i.

Example 4: Scale a complex number
Compute −3(2+4i).
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: −6−12i.

Example 5: Multiply complex binomials
Multiply (2+3i)(4−i).
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: 11+10i, because i²=−1.

Example 6: Take complex conjugates
Find conjugates of 5−2i and −3i.
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: 5+2i and 3i.

Example 7: Divide using conjugate
Compute (2+3i)/(1−i) in standard complex form.
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: (−1/2)+(5/2)i by multiplying numerator/denominator by (1+i).

Example 8: Substitute complex input in polynomial
For f(z)=z²+2z+1, calculate f(2+i).
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: (2+i)²+2(2+i)+1=8+6i.

Example 9: Substitute complex input in rational function
For g(z)=(z+2)/(z+1), evaluate g(i).
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: (2+i)/(1+i)=(3−i)/2.

Example 10: Reduce high power of i
Evaluate i^37 using the four-step cycle.
Method: Use standard complex algebra and i²=−1; show exact real/imaginary components.
Answer: i because 37≡1 mod4.

Translations.Title: Quadratic Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Original source objectives: identify a parabola’s axis, vertex and intercepts; convert general and vertex forms; determine domain/range and maxima/minima; find complex and real roots; model constrained quadratic optimization.

A quadratic f(x)=ax²+bx+c (a≠0) has axis x=−b/(2a). Writing f(x)=a(x−h)²+k exposes vertex (h,k) and its maximum or minimum.

For intercepts set x=0 for y and set f(x)=0 for x. The discriminant Δ=b²−4ac determines real intersections versus complex conjugate solutions.

The vertex controls range and optimizes a maximum area, revenue or height when its x-value lies in the physical model’s admissible domain.

For projectile formulas, report both algebraic roots but reject negative physical time and state units.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) Rewrite 2x²−12x+11 in vertex form. (b) Find real/complex roots of x²+4=0. (c) Maximize R(p)=−3p²+90p under p≥0.

Independent Try It 1 — Vertex from graph. A parabola has vertex (1,−3) and passes through (2,−1). Find its equation.

Independent Try It 2 — Complete square. Rewrite x²−4x+7 in vertex form.

Independent Try It 3 — Domain and range. Determine range of −2(x+3)²+5.

Independent Try It 4 — Solve real and complex roots. Find roots of 2x²−4x+5.

Independent Try It 5 — Projectile optimization. h(t)=−16t²+96t+112. Find peak time and height; positive impact time.

Positive Δ two distinct real, zero double real, negative two nonreal conjugates.

Use vertex form to read transformed y=x².

Reject nonphysical negative-time projectile root.

Translations.Title: Power Functions and Polynomial Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: identify power functions and their end behavior; identify polynomials; find polynomial degree and leading coefficient.

A power function is a single term a·x^n. Polynomial functions are finite sums of nonnegative integer powers with real coefficients.

At large |x|, the leading term dominates: even-degree tails have the same sign, odd-degree tails opposite signs. For positive leading coefficients, the right tail rises; negative falls.

Factors reveal real zeros. At a zero of odd multiplicity the curve crosses the horizontal axis; at even multiplicity it touches or bounces.

A degree-n polynomial has at most n distinct real zeros and at most n−1 turning points, and a polynomial graph is continuous and smooth.

Independent Edulytics cool-down: (a) Is 4x³−2x a single power function? (b) Determine tails for −2x⁷+5x². (c) Find degree and real zeros of 3x(x−1)²(x+2).

Independent Try It 1 — Classify polynomial and power. Is 2x²·4x³ a power function? Is x⁵−x a power function?

Independent Try It 2 — Even negative power tails. State end behavior of −5x⁴.

Independent Try It 3 — Leading coefficient after rearranging. For 4x²−x⁶+2x−6 determine degree and leading coefficient.

Independent Try It 4 — Least degree from turning points. A smooth continuous curve changes direction 3 times and tails both rise. What minimum polynomial degree is possible?

Independent Try It 5 — Expand factors and infer tails. Find leading term and degree of 0.2(x−2)(x+1)(x−5).

Independent Try It 6 — Find polynomial zeros. Find intercepts of f(x)=2x³−6x²−20x.

Independent Try It 7 — Maximum turning point count. For degree12 polynomial, state max x-intercepts and turning points.

Independent Try It 8 — Use graph root multiplicity. A polynomial graph touches at x=2 and crosses at x=−1. Find a simple polynomial model.

Independent Try It 9 — Crossing behavior from factors. For f(x)=0.2(x−2)(x+1)(x−5), state intercept crossing behavior.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Power function
One term a·xⁿ with constant a and exponent n≥0 for polynomial power functions.
The exponent is power, a its coefficient.
−3x⁵.

Polynomial definition
Finite sum of nonnegative integer powers of x with real coefficients.
Fractional or negative x powers are not polynomials.
2x³−x+7.

Degree
Largest exponent with nonzero coefficient.
Product degrees add unless zero polynomial factors.
x²(x−1) degree3.

Leading coefficient
Coefficient of the highest-degree term.
Leading term determines both end behaviors.
−2x⁶+5 has leading coefficient −2.

Even-degree behavior
Both tails of a polynomial travel in the same vertical direction.
Sign of leading coefficient decides up or down.
−x⁴ → both down.

Odd-degree behavior
Polynomial tails travel in opposite vertical directions.
Positive leading→left down/right up.
x³ → down-left/up-right.

Roots and intercepts
An x-intercept has p(x)=0; y-intercept p(0).
Factored form makes zeros explicit.
(x−2)(x+1) roots 2,−1.

Multiplicity
Odd root multiplicity crosses x-axis, even multiplicity touches/bounces.
Graph behavior near a root depends on multiplicity parity.
(x−2)² touches at2.

Turning point bound
Degree n≥1 polynomial has at most n−1 turning points.
Number of distinct real roots at most n.
Degree5 max4 turns.

Continuity/smoothness
Polynomial graphs are continuous and smooth without corners or discontinuities.
A graph with a hole or jump cannot be a polynomial graph.
x³−4x is continuous.

Calling x⁻² a polynomial.
Why: Exponent is a negative integer.
Correction: Polynomial powers must be nonnegative integers.

Concluding root multiplicity from leading sign.

Why: n is only the maximum; some roots can be complex or repeated.

2. Degree is highest nonzero power and leading coefficient controls tails.

3. Odd/even degree determines whether tails match.

4. Factorization gives roots and multiplicities.

5. Degree n bounds real zeros and turning points.

Translations.Title: Graphs of Polynomial Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals: distinguish smooth polynomial graphs from graphs with corners or discontinuities, factor to find zeros, recognize multiplicities, determine tails and turning-point bounds, sketch graphs and apply the Intermediate Value Theorem.

Polynomial p(x)=a∏(x−r)^m describes zeros and their multiplicities: odd m crosses the x-axis, even m touches it.

The leading coefficient and parity of total degree govern tails. A degree n polynomial has at most n−1 turning points; these are limits, not guaranteed counts.

When a continuous polynomial changes sign across an interval, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees at least one root inside, without claiming its exact position.

Construct a formula by multiplying factors corresponding to roots and use a known y-intercept or another coordinate to determine the scale a.

For optimization, compare all critical points in the physical interval plus endpoints; a local extremum alone may not be globally optimal.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) Describe end behavior and root multiplicity of −(x−2)²(x+1). (b) Show x³−x−1 has a zero in (1,2). (c) Construct a quadratic with double zero at3 and y-intercept8.

Independent Try It 1 — Root/axis intercepts. Find all real x-intercepts of p(x)=x⁴−10x²+9 and y-intercept.

Independent Try It 2 — Use multiplicity graph. A polynomial has simple zero x=−2, double zero x=1, another simple zero x=3. Explain crossing/touching.

Independent Try It 3 — Sketch given factors. Sketch p(x)=x(x−1)⁴(x+3)³ and classify tails.

Independent Try It 4 — Apply IVT with sign change. Show p(x)=x³−2x−2 has a real zero between x1 and x2.

Independent Try It 5 — Build from a graph description. A degree3 polynomial crosses at x=−1, touches at x=2 and passes through (0,8). Find lowest-degree formula.

Independent Try It 6 — Local extrema on interval. For f(x)=x³−3x on [−2,2], find global max/min including endpoints.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Polynomial graph continuity
Polynomials are continuous at every real input.
No finite jumps, gaps or vertical asymptotes.
x³−x.

Smoothness
Polynomial graphs have derivatives of all orders.
Sharp corners suggest non-polynomial rules.
|x| is not polynomial.

Root factorization
p(r)=0 iff (x−r) divides p(x).
Find real x-intercepts from factored p(x).
(x−2)(x+1) zeros2,−1.

Multiplicity
Factor (x−r)^m establishes root multiplicity m.
Even m touches, odd m crosses.
(x−1)² touches x1.

Leading term tails
Degree parity and sign of leading coefficient determine end behavior.
Even: same direction, odd: opposite.
−x³ left up/right down.

Y-intercept
Evaluate p(0) for y-intercept.
Often use it to determine unknown scalar factor.
a(x−1)(x+2) at zero −2a.

Polynomial turning-point bound
Degree n polynomial has at most n−1 turning points.
No claim that maximum number must occur.
Degree5 at most4 turns.

Intermediate Value Theorem
A continuous function whose values at a and b have opposite signs has a zero in (a,b).
Show f(a)f(b)<0 and cite continuity.
x³−3x−1 signs change between1 and2.

Polynomial reconstruction
Use zeros, multiplicities and a known nonzero point to determine scale.
p(x)=a∏(x−r)^m.
Zeros simple−1, double3 lead degree3.

Local versus global extrema
Local maxima/minima can differ from interval-wide extrema.
Check interval endpoints and interior critical points.
x³−3x on [−2,2].

Example 2: Factor a polynomial for its real zeros

Translations.Title: Dividing Polynomials
Translations.Explanation:
Learning goals from authorized source: use long division and synthetic division to divide polynomials.

The polynomial division identity p=dq+r requires either zero remainder or a remainder of degree lower than the divisor.

Long division: divide leading terms, multiply the divisor, subtract, and bring down the next coefficient; keep each polynomial degree aligned.

Synthetic division requires a divisor x−k, uses the coefficient sequence including zeros for omitted powers, and outputs quotient coefficients followed by the remainder.

For ax+b divisors use long division directly or transform to x−k and adjust the quotient by the leading scale a.

Use polynomial quotient in geometric volume/area applications only where all divisor dimensions are nonzero and admissible.

Independent Edulytics cool-down: (a) Divide x³−3x²−4x+12 by x−3. (b) Divide 2x²+5x+2 by 2x+1. (c) Explain why zero remainder confirms a factor.

Independent Try It 1 — General long division. Divide 3x³−5x²+2x+10 by x+2.

Independent Try It 2 — Synthetic division with missing term. Divide 2x⁴−3x²+7 by x−1.

Independent Try It 3 — Find geometric missing side. A rectangle area A=(x+4)(3x−2) and width w=x+4; find its length.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Polynomial division identity
For nonzero divisor d(x), p(x)=d(x)q(x)+r(x), deg(r)<deg(d).
Always verify by multiplying back.
x²−1=(x−1)(x+1).

Long division
Divide leading term, multiply, subtract, carry down, repeat.
Continue while remainder degree ≥ divisor degree.
(2x²+7x+3)/(x+3)=2x+1.

Synthetic division
Shortcut for divisor x−k with coefficient row including zero placeholders.
Use k with sign opposite binomial constant.
x+2 uses k=−2.

Missing coefficients
A missing x^j term has coefficient zero in synthetic division.
Do not shift powers accidentally.
x⁴+3x²−4 has [1,0,3,0,−4].

Remainder theorem preview
Division by x−k leaves constant remainder p(k).
Zero remainder means x−k divides p.
p(1)=0 ⇒ x−1 factor.

Nonmonic divisor
For ax+b factor, synthetic divide by x−(−b/a) and scale quotient by 1/a.
Direct long division also works.
Divide by 3x−1, root k=1/3.

Polynomial factor test
A zero remainder certifies exact divisibility.
Nonzero remainder cannot be silently ignored.
x³−1 divisible by x−1.

Complex synthetic root
Synthetic division with complex k can produce complex quotient coefficients.
Keep real and imaginary parts exact.
x²+1 divisible by x−i.

Geometric applications
Unknown height or width comes from volume/area divided by known dimensions.
State physical restrictions such as nonzero positive lengths.
H=V/(LW).
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Polynomial long division by a monic binomial
Divide 2x²+7x+3 by x+3, including remainder.
Method: Use polynomial long/synthetic division and check dividend=divisor×quotient+remainder.
Answer: 2x+1, remainder0, because (x+3)(2x+1)=2x²+7x+3.

Example 2: Polynomial long division by a general linear divisor
Divide 6x³+7x²−16x+3 by 3x−1.
Method: Use polynomial long/synthetic division and check dividend=divisor×quotient+remainder.
Answer: Quotient 2x²+3x−13/3, remainder −4/3; verify dividend=divisor·quotient+remainder.

Example 3: Set up synthetic division correctly
Divide x³−4x²+x+6 by x−2 using coefficient row [1,−4,1,6].
Method: Use polynomial long/synthetic division and check dividend=divisor×quotient+remainder.
Answer: Quotient x²−2x−3, remainder0; synthetic parameter k=2.

Example 4: Synthetic division with negative k
Divide x³+2x²−5x−6 by x+1.
Method: Use polynomial long/synthetic division and check dividend=divisor×quotient+remainder.
Answer: Quotient x²+x−6, remainder0; k=−1.

Example 5: Synthetic division with missing powers
Divide x⁴+3x²−4 by x−1, including zero coefficients for x³ and x.
Method: Use polynomial long/synthetic division and check dividend=divisor×quotient+remainder.
Answer: Quotient x³+x²+4x+4, remainder0.

Example 6: Use volume-to-height division
A rectangular prism has volume V=(x+2)(x−1)(2x+3) cubic units; length (x+2), width (x−1). Find height.
Method: Use polynomial long/synthetic division and check dividend=divisor×quotient+remainder.
Answer: Height H(x)=2x+3 units with x>1 for positive dimensions.

Step 3: Validate: Reconstruct exact dividend from quotient, divisor and remainder.

6. Use volume-to-height division

Translations.CommonMistakes:
Use k=+2 for dividing by x+2.
Why: Synthetic k is the root x=−2.
Correction: Write divisor as x−(−2).

Omit zero coefficients in synthetic division.
Why: Misaligns polynomial powers and corrupts quotient.
Correction: Include a zero for each missing degree.

Ignore a nonzero remainder.
Why: Division identity is then false.
Correction: State quotient and remainder and verify by multiplication.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Division identity p=dq+r must be preserved.

2. Long division works for every nonzero polynomial divisor.

3. Synthetic division shortcut uses x−k and zero coefficient placeholders.

4. Remainder zero implies exact factor.

5. Geometric quotients require physically valid dimensions.

Translations.Title: Zeros of Polynomial Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Original source learning goals: evaluate a polynomial via remainder theorem, apply factor theorem and Rational Zero Theorem, find real/complex roots, construct factors, analyze Descartes sign changes and solve polynomial volume models.

The Remainder Theorem says division by x−k leaves p(k); the Factor Theorem specializes this to zero remainder. Rational roots must be tested, not assumed.

The Rational Zero Theorem gives possible fractions ±(factor of constant)/(factor of leading coefficient), reduced to lowest terms.

Nonreal zeros of real-coefficient polynomials occur in conjugate pairs. All n complex roots of degree n are counted with multiplicity.

Descartes' Rule of Signs restricts possible positive/negative real zero counts but does not identify roots; explicitly test candidates.

Contextual models such as cubic volume require rejecting nonpositive lengths or other impossible roots.

Independent Edulytics cool-down: (a) Find remainder of x³−2x²+5x−4 on division by x−1. (b) Factor x³−6x²+11x−6. (c) Construct monic polynomial with roots 2,±i.

Independent Try It 1 — Remainder at negative input. Find remainder of p(x)=x³−4x²+x+7 divided by x+2.

Independent Try It 2 — Factor theorem with known root. Find zeros of p(x)=x³−5x²+2x+8 given x−2 is a factor.

Independent Try It 3 — Rational zero possibilities. List possible rational zeros of 3x³−4x²−7x+2.

Independent Try It 4 — Find real and complex zeros. Solve p(x)=x³−x²+9x−9.

Independent Try It 5 — Real coefficients conjugate pair. Build monic cubic with zeros −2,3i,−3i.

Independent Try It 6 — Descartes sign possibilities. For p(x)=x⁴−2x³−x²+4x−4, give allowed positive and negative root counts.

Independent Try It 7 — Box model polynomial dimensions. A box height h, width h+1, length 2h+1 has volume30 cubic units. Find positive h and dimensions.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Remainder Theorem
Remainder on division by x−k equals p(k).
Evaluate directly rather than perform full division.
p(2)=7.

Factor Theorem
x−k is a factor iff p(k)=0.
Zero remainder certifies root/factor.
p(2)=0 ⇒ x−2.

Rational Zero Theorem
For integer coefficients, any reduced rational root a/b has a dividing constant and b dividing leading coefficient.
Candidates need testing; some roots irrational or complex.
p=2x³−5x²−4x+3 candidates ±1,±3,±1/2,±3/2.

Synthetic root testing
Substitute candidate and divide to lower polynomial degree.
Repeat a root to detect multiplicity.
(x−1)² repeated root.

Linear factorization
Polynomial over complex numbers factors into degree1 factors counting multiplicity.
Real-coefficient polynomials have nonreal conjugate pairs.
x²+4=(x−2i)(x+2i).

Complex conjugate zeros
If coefficients are real and a+bi is a root with b≠0, a−bi also is.
Multiply conjugate factors into real quadratic.
(x−1)²+4.

Descartes' Rule of Signs
Positive real zero count equals sign changes of p(x), or less by an even integer.
Negative real zero count uses sign changes of p(−x).
3 sign changes allows3 or1.

Polynomial from zeros
Multiply (x−r) factors and solve scale from a known point.
Repeated roots use powers and nonreal roots paired for real coefficients.
p=a(x−2)²(x+1).

Polynomial volume model
Combine dimensional expressions with volume=length×width×height.
Use only positive physical roots and correct units.
w(w+4)(w/3)=351.

Treating each Rational Zero Theorem candidate as an actual root.

Translations.Title: Rational Functions
Translations.Explanation:
A rational function is a quotient of polynomials; the original denominator cannot be zero, even where a common factor cancels.

Arrow notation x→a− or x→a+ describes one-sided input behavior. A vertical asymptote often signals diverging output, while a removable discontinuity is a finite-valued hole.

After factoring numerator and denominator, cancel common factors to locate holes but retain original domain exclusions. Remaining real denominator zeros yield vertical asymptotes.

Horizontal asymptotes follow degree comparison: numerator degree lower gives y=0; equal gives the ratio of leading coefficients; higher generally requires polynomial division for polynomial end behavior.

A graph can cross a horizontal asymptote but does not take values at a vertical asymptote's x-coordinate; a hole is an excluded point on the simplified curve.

Use intercepts, limits, sign charts and asymptotes to sketch each branch. Contextual units and positive-domain restrictions are essential in rational models.

Independent Try It 1: For f(x)=−1/(x+4), determine f(x) as x→−4− and x→−4+.

Independent Try It 2: For g(x)=3/(x−1)−2 identify both asymptotes.

Independent Try It 3: A tank holds 30 g in 60 L; add 3 g/min and 2 L/min. Write c(t) and its long-run level.

Independent Try It 4: Find domain of (x−5)/(x²−16).

Independent Try It 5: For (x²−9)/(x−3), locate the hole.

Independent Try It 6: Find end asymptote for (4x²+3)/(x²+1).

Independent Try It 7: Find x/y intercepts of (x+3)/(x−2).

Independent Try It 8: Construct a rational function with zero x=2, vertical asymptote x=−1, horizontal asymptote y=3.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (1) Analyze f(x)=(x²−4)/(x²+x−6) for its original domain, hole, vertical and horizontal asymptotes. (2) Analyze g(x)=(x−1)²/((x+2)(x−3)) for zeros, poles, multiplicities, horizontal asymptote and y-intercept. (3) A tank contains 5 kg solute in 50 L and receives 1 kg solute and 5 L liquid per minute: write C(t), domain and long-run concentration.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Rational function and domain
A quotient p(x)/q(x), q(x)≠0.
Exclude every zero of the original denominator.
(x−2)/(x²−4) excludes x=−2 and x=2.

Removable hole
A common factor cancels while its root remains excluded from the domain.
Evaluate the simplified expression at the excluded input to find the hole's y-coordinate.
(x−2)(x+3)/((x−2)(x+1)) has hole (2,5/3).

Vertical asymptote
A vertical line where the function grows unbounded on at least one side.
Check uncancelled real denominator factors and one-sided behavior.
1/(x+2) has vertical x=−2.

Horizontal/slant asymptotes
Lines approached as input grows without bound.
Use degree comparisons and long division; horizontal lines may be crossed.
(x²+2x+3)/(x+1)=x+1+2/(x+1).

Step 3: Validate: Divide total solute mass by total volume; compare leading coefficients.

4. Domain restrictions
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: All real x except −3 and 3.
Step 3: Validate: Factor denominator (x−3)(x+3); never include zero-denominator points.

5. Vertical asymptotes
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: x=2 and x=−4.
Step 3: Validate: Neither denominator factor cancels with the numerator.

6. Hole versus asymptote
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: Hole at (2,5/3); vertical asymptote x=−1; domain excludes both 2 and −1.
Step 3: Validate: Cancel only to compute the limit; original function remains undefined at x=2.

7. Slant asymptote
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: f(x)=x+1+2/(x+1); slant asymptote y=x+1.
Step 3: Validate: Polynomial division gives the linear quotient and vanishing remainder ratio.

8. Horizontal asymptote
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: y=3/2.
Step 3: Validate: Equal polynomial degrees: leading coefficient ratio.

9. All vertical and horizontal asymptotes
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: Vertical asymptotes x=−2, x=2; horizontal y=1; zeros x=±1.
Step 3: Validate: Factor numerator and denominator and compare degrees.

10. Intercepts of rational function
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: x-intercept (4,0), y-intercept (0,−2), vertical x=−2, horizontal y=1.
Step 3: Validate: Numerator zero produces x-intercept only if denominator nonzero.

11. Graph from critical points
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: Intercept (0,0); vertical x=±1; horizontal y=0. On (1,∞) graph is positive, on (0,1) negative.
Step 3: Validate: Use signs between critical inputs to place branches.

12. Construct a rational function
Step 1: Plan: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Step 2: f(x)=2(x−1)/((x+2)(x−3)).
Step 3: Validate: Choose factored numerator/denominator and solve f(0)=1/3 for scale.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Treating a cancelled factor as an allowed input.
Why: Cancelling does not restore undefined domain values.
Correction: Keep the original denominator restrictions and graph a hole.

Claiming every horizontal asymptote is uncrossable.
Why: Horizontal asymptotes describe end behavior, not forbidden output values.
Correction: Solve f(x)=asymptote value and check any finite intersections.

Forgetting that a denominator zero may create a hole.
Why: A common numerator factor cancels and leaves finite limit.
Correction: Factor first and distinguish cancelled from remaining factors.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Original denominator zeros are always excluded.

2. Cancel common factors to distinguish holes from vertical asymptotes.

3. A horizontal asymptote can be crossed.

4. Use intercepts and branch signs in addition to asymptotes.

5. Context models require units and permissible input ranges.

6. Cool-down requires factor cancellation without restoring excluded inputs, pole/root multiplicities, and consistent application units.

Translations.Title: Inverses and Radical Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Original section skills: invert polynomial and rational functions, restrict non-one-to-one polynomial domains, invert radicals, analyze composed radical-rational domains and apply inverse models.

An inverse reflects ordered pairs across y=x. Always compare the original domain with the inverse range.

For quadratic inverses, impose the original increasing or decreasing branch before choosing the sign of a square root.

For radical or rational expressions, keep the original exclusions; clearing denominators and squaring may introduce invalid candidates.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) invert f(x)=(x+2)² on x≥−2; (b) invert f(x)=√(x−4)+3; (c) find domain of √((x−1)/(x+2)).

Independent Try It 1: For f(x)=x³−5, write f⁻¹ and verify by composition.

Independent Try It 2: Find inverse of f(x)=(x+1)² on x≥−1.

Independent Try It 3: Find inverse of f(x)=(x−2)² on x≤2.

Independent Try It 4: Invert f(x)=1+√(3x−6).

Independent Try It 5: Invert f(x)=(2x−3)/(x+4).
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Inverse functions
Interchange inputs and outputs; an inverse function exists if the original is one-to-one on its stated domain.
Verify both compositions and exchange domain/range.
f(x)=2x−7 has inverse (x+7)/2.

Restricted quadratic inverse
A full parabola is not one-to-one; restrict to one monotone branch.
The original branch determines ±√ after swapping x and y.
f(x)=(x−4)², x≥4 has inverse 4+√x.

Radical inverse
Undo the radical with squaring/cubing, but preserve range and domain restrictions.
Squaring may introduce extraneous roots; always check against original range.
f(x)=√(x−1)+2 inverse (x−2)²+1, x≥2.

Inverse rational functions
Swap x,y then solve linearly for x; exclude denominator zeros in original and inverse.
Check impossible horizontal-asymptote outputs are not in inverse domain.
(3x+1)/(x−2) has inverse (2x+1)/(x−3).

Radical rational domains
A square root requires nonnegative radicand and nonzero original denominator.
Use a sign chart of numerator zeros and denominator poles.
√((x−2)/(x+3)) permits x<−3 or x≥2.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Verify inverse functions
Show f(x)=2x−7 and g(x)=(x+7)/2 are inverses.
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: f(g(x))=x and g(f(x))=x after simplifying both compositions.

Example 2: Inverse cubic polynomial
Invert f(x)=3x³+1 over real numbers.
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: Solve y=3x³+1 to get f⁻¹(y)=∛((y−1)/3).

Example 3: Domain-restricted quadratic
Find inverse of f(x)=(x−4)² for x≥4.
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: Its inverse is f⁻¹(y)=4+√y for y≥0; the positive square-root branch follows original restriction.

Example 4: Choose a quadratic inverse branch
Invert f(x)=6−(x+2)² for x≥−2.
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: f⁻¹(y)=−2+√(6−y) for y≤6; inverse outputs are ≥−2.

Example 5: Inverse radical with domain
Invert f(x)=2+√(x−1).
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: f⁻¹(y)=(y−2)²+1, inverse input y≥2; original input x≥1.

Example 6: Cone application
A cone has height twice its radius and volume V=2πr³/3. Find r for V=18π.
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: r=∛(3V/(2π)); V=18π gives r=3 and height6 length units.

Example 7: Radical of rational domain
Find domain of h(x)=√((x−2)/(x+3)).
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: Require (x−2)/(x+3)≥0 and x≠−3: (−∞,−3) ∪ [2,∞).

Example 8: Inverse rational function
Invert f(x)=(3x+1)/(x−2).
Method: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Answer: Solve y(x−2)=3x+1: inverse f⁻¹(y)=(2y+1)/(y−3), y≠3.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions:
1. Verify inverse functions
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: f(g(x))=x and g(f(x))=x after simplifying both compositions.
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.

2. Inverse cubic polynomial
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: Solve y=3x³+1 to get f⁻¹(y)=∛((y−1)/3).
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.

3. Domain-restricted quadratic
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: Its inverse is f⁻¹(y)=4+√y for y≥0; the positive square-root branch follows original restriction.
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.

4. Choose a quadratic inverse branch
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: f⁻¹(y)=−2+√(6−y) for y≤6; inverse outputs are ≥−2.
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.

5. Inverse radical with domain
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: f⁻¹(y)=(y−2)²+1, inverse input y≥2; original input x≥1.
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.

6. Cone application
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: r=∛(3V/(2π)); V=18π gives r=3 and height6 length units.
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.

7. Radical of rational domain
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: Require (x−2)/(x+3)≥0 and x≠−3: (−∞,−3) ∪ [2,∞).
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.

8. Inverse rational function
Step 1: Plan: Reverse input/output, solve and respect one-to-one domain restrictions.
Step 2: Solve y(x−2)=3x+1: inverse f⁻¹(y)=(2y+1)/(y−3), y≠3.
Step 3: Validate: Recompose and verify original domain/range restrictions.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Use both square-root branches for a single inverse function.
Why: Without an original domain restriction a parabola is not one-to-one.
Correction: Choose branch based on the restricted original domain.

Ignore radical output constraints when inverting.
Why: Squaring can introduce invalid extraneous cases.
Correction: Record inverse domain from original range and check.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Verify inverse compositions.

2. Restrict quadratics to monotone branch.

3. Exchange domain and range.

4. Keep radical and denominator restrictions.

5. Interpret inverse models with physical units.

6. Cool-down reviews a restricted quadratic inverse, a radical inverse, and real-radicand sign restrictions.

Translations.Title: Modeling Using Variation
Translations.Explanation:
Three original-source goals: model direct, inverse, and joint variation, determine the shared constant and evaluate the model at changed inputs.

Direct variation is y=kxⁿ; for n=1 the graph is a line through the origin. For other powers the graph may be nonlinear even though variation is direct.

Inverse variation is y=k/xⁿ, where x≠0, and its graph displays domain exclusions and decreasing or increasing branch behavior depending on signs and powers.

Joint variation uses a single nonzero constant of variation and products of powers or quotients; use source values to find k and preserve physical units.

An applied law can have direct dependence on some variables and inverse dependence on others; do not confuse 'inverse variation' with 'inverse function'.

Independent first-party Cool-down: (a) Model revenue varying directly with units. (b) Model light intensity varying inversely with squared distance. (c) A jointly varying force F=kv²A is calibrated and evaluated.

Independent Try It 1: y varies directly as x². When x=3, y=18. Find y for x=5.

Independent Try It 2: y varies inversely as x³. When x=2, y=24. Find y for x=4.

Independent Try It 3: q varies directly as a²b and inversely as c. If q=12 at a=2,b=3,c=2, find q at a=3,b=4,c=6.

Figure-skill alternative 1: Original publisher Figure 1 illustrates earnings y=0.16s; a first-party alternative uses e=0.1s, s∈{0,200,400,600}, e∈{0,20,40,60}. Constant positive rate leads to origin line and proportional increases.

Figure-skill alternative 2: Original source Figure 2 illustrates y=(25/8)x³ at x=2 and x=6; independent first-party graph uses y=2x³ with points (0,0),(1,2),(2,16),(3,54). Higher-power direct variation curves even though multiplier k remains constant.

Figure-skill alternative 3: Original Figure 3 illustrates a reciprocal form. Independent alternative y=24/x for x>0 with (1,24),(2,12),(3,8),(6,4). Doubling x halves y for inverse first-power variation.

Figure-skill alternative 4: Original Figure 4 illustrates inverse cube y=200/x³. Independent alternative y=64/x³ for x>0, points (2,8),(4,1),(8,1/8). Doubling x divides output by 8 and the x=0 domain exclusion remains.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Direct variation
y=kxⁿ for a specified n and k≠0.
Compute k=y/xⁿ, x≠0.
y=3x².

Inverse variation
y=k/xⁿ, x≠0.
Compute k=yxⁿ.
y=12/x².

Joint variation
One quantity is proportional to a product or quotient of powers of multiple quantities.
Use one constant k, not one per independent variable.
F=kv²A.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Direct variation and commission
Commission C varies directly with sale price s. If a sale of $5000 pays $400, find C for a $7500 sale.
Method: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Answer: k=400/5000=0.08; C=0.08s; for s=7500, C=$600.

Example 2: Power variation
y varies directly with x cubed. If y=16 at x=2, find y at x=4.
Method: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Answer: k=16/8=2; y=2x³, so y(4)=128.

Example 3: Inverse variation
Intensity varies inversely with square of distance. If I=27 at distance 2 m, find I at distance 6 m.
Method: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Answer: k=27×4=108, I=108/d²; at d=6, I=3.

Example 4: Joint variation
Cost C varies jointly with workers w and hours h and inversely with productivity p. If C=60 when w=3,h=4,p=2, compute C for w=5,h=6,p=3.
Method: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Answer: C=kwh/p, k=60×2/(3×4)=10; C=10×5×6/3=100.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions:
1. Direct variation and commission
Step 1: Plan: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Step 2: k=400/5000=0.08; C=0.08s; for s=7500, C=$600.
Step 3: Validate: Substitute the calibration point and verify the resulting constant.

2. Power variation
Step 1: Plan: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Step 2: k=16/8=2; y=2x³, so y(4)=128.
Step 3: Validate: Substitute the calibration point and verify the resulting constant.

3. Inverse variation
Step 1: Plan: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Step 2: k=27×4=108, I=108/d²; at d=6, I=3.
Step 3: Validate: Substitute the calibration point and verify the resulting constant.

4. Joint variation
Step 1: Plan: Translate variation wording, solve k from a measured point, substitute the target values and check units.
Step 2: C=kwh/p, k=60×2/(3×4)=10; C=10×5×6/3=100.
Step 3: Validate: Substitute the calibration point and verify the resulting constant.
Translations.CommonMistakes:
Model all direct variation with y=kx only.
Why: Direct powers x², x³ and radicals are valid models.
Correction: Preserve the specified exponent n.

Assign separate constants to each jointly varying factor.
Why: A joint variation law uses one k.
Correction: Write y=kx^az^b/w^c then solve k once.
Translations.QuickSummary:
1. Identify direct/inverse/joint dependence and powers.

2. Use one constant k.

3. Check dimensions and calibration measurements.

4. Direct variation may be nonlinear for powers other than one.

5. Avoid conflating inverse variation and inverse function.

Translations.Title: Exponential Functions
Translations.Explanation:
An exponential function has the form f(x)=a·b^x (a≠0, b>0, b≠1). Its base is a repeated ratio, unlike constant differences in linear models.

Evaluate powers first, then products and translations. With positive a, b>1 means exponential growth and 0<b<1 means exponential decay.

To fit a model, infer b from output ratios over equal changes in x and solve a from one given point. A table with constant differences is linear; constant nonzero ratios can be exponential.

Compound interest uses A=P(1+r/n)^(nt), where the APR r is a decimal, n is compoundings per year and t is measured in years.

Continuous compounding A=Pe^(rt), while continuous growth or decay models are f(t)=ae^(kt) with k positive for growth and negative for decay.

Currency results should be rounded only after evaluating the full expression; for population and physical quantities, include units and context.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: identify whether 5(1.2)^x is growth, fit exponential with f(0)=3 and f(2)=48, and calculate continuous interest on $1000 for 2 years at 4%.

Independent Try It 1: Classify x^4, (3/4)^x, and 7x.

Independent Try It 2: Find 2·3^(x−1)+1 at x=3.

Independent Try It 3: A city has 20,000 people growing 2% annually. Model 5-year population.

Independent Try It 4: A bacteria culture starts at 200 and doubles every 3 hours. Express count at t hours.

Independent Try It 5: Exponential f(0)=7 and f(2)=63. Find model.

Independent Try It 6: Given graph points (0,6),(1,18),(2,54), write f.

Independent Try It 7: Table y=4,12,36 at x=1,2,3. Find f=ab^x.

Independent Try It 8: Find amount of $1,000 at 8% APR compounded twice annually for 2 years.

Independent Try It 9: What deposit gives $5000 after 1 year at 12% compounded monthly?

Independent Try It 10: Evaluate e²/2.

Independent Try It 11: Find $2,000 after 3 years at 3% continuous interest.

Independent Try It 12: Mass starts at 60 and decays at 10% continuous rate. Find after 5 units.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Exponential function
f(x)=a·b^x, a≠0, b>0 and b≠1.
An exponential has constant output ratio for equal input increments.
f(x)=4·2^x.

Growth and decay
With positive initial amount, exponential base b>1 grows, 0<b<1 decays.
B=1+r for growth by fraction r, B=1−r for decay.
200(1.08)^t or 200(0.92)^t.

Compound interest
A=P(1+r/n)^(nt).
Nominal APR r as decimal; n annual periods, t years; P and A share currency.
1200(1+0.06/4)^12.

Natural exponential
e≈2.718281828; continuous compounding or natural exponential model.
For A=Pe^(rt), rate r=0.05 means 5% per year.
3500e^(0.2).
Translations.WorkedExamples:
Example 1: Recognize an exponential function
Which is exponential: 5x², 5(2)^x, or 5x+2?
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: The function 5(2)^x is exponential: x is in the exponent and base 2 is positive and not 1.

Example 2: Evaluate powers and order
Evaluate g(x)=3·2^(x+1)−4 at x=2.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: g(2)=3·2³−4=20.

Example 3: Interpret a growth model
A colony starts at 500 cells and grows 8% per hour. Model and predict after 3 hours.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: N(t)=500(1.08)^t; N(3)=500(1.08)³≈629.856 cells. Counts may be rounded to 630.

Example 4: Find model with known initial value
An investment is worth 800 initially and rises by factor 1.1 annually. Write value function.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: V(t)=800(1.1)^t for t≥0. Initial value V(0)=800.

Example 5: Find exponential function from two points
An exponential f(x)=ab^x satisfies f(1)=6 and f(3)=54. Find f.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: f(3)/f(1)=b²=9 so b=3; a=6/3=2. f(x)=2·3^x.

Example 6: Model graph intercept and ratio
Exponential graph has y-intercept 4 and points (1,8),(2,16). Find function.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: f(x)=4·2^x, with positive range and horizontal asymptote y=0.

Example 7: Fit exponential sequence from data
Observed readings x=0,1,2,3 are 5,15,45,135. Fit model.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: Ratio 3 per unit, f(x)=5·3^x. Check all four observations.

Example 8: Evaluate compound interest
Deposit $1,200 at APR 6% compounded quarterly for 3 years. Find amount.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: A=1200(1+0.06/4)^(4·3)=1200(1.015)^12≈$1434.74.

Example 9: Solve compound interest for principal
What principal yields $2,000 after 2 years at 4% compounded monthly?
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: P=2000/(1+0.04/12)^(24)≈$1846.48 (calculate before rounding).

Example 10: Evaluate natural exponential
Evaluate 2e^(−1) to four decimal places.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: 2/e≈0.7358.

Example 11: Continuous compounding growth
Deposit $3,500 at 5% compounded continuously for 4 years.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: A=3500e^(0.05·4)=3500e^0.2≈$4274.91.

Example 12: Continuous decay
A 100 g sample decays continuously at rate 0.07 per hour. Find 6-hour mass.
Method: Use exact exponential model, ratio, domain and appropriate units.
Answer: M(t)=100e^(−0.07t), so M(6)=100e^(−0.42)≈65.7047 g.

Treat APR 6% as 6 in an exponent.
Why: APR must be a decimal (0.06).

Translations.Title: Graphs of Exponential Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Exponential graphs f(x)=a·b^x have domain all real values and, when a>0, strictly positive outputs; their horizontal asymptote is y=0.

For f(x)=a·b^(x−h)+k, horizontal translation h and vertical translation k move the asymptote to y=k. A negative a reflects across the horizontal baseline.

Reflection across the y-axis replaces x by −x; f(−x) changes growth direction without changing the y-intercept.

A vertical scale factor multiplies the distances of curve points from their baseline; use transformed anchor points and explicit range/domain.

To estimate solutions of a b^x+d=c graphically, locate curve/line intersection, then refine numerically to the required precision.

Translations.Title: Logarithmic Functions
Translations.Explanation:
A logarithm is an exponent: log_b(x)=y if and only if b^y=x, with b>0, b!=1 and x>0.

y=b^x and y=log_b(x) are inverse functions. Their coordinates swap across the line y=x; the logarithm has domain (0,infinity), range all real, and vertical asymptote x=0.

Negative and zero inputs have no real logarithm. Negative logarithm outputs are allowed; log_b(1)=0 and log_b(b)=1.

Common log means log_10; natural log ln means log_e. Use 10^(log x)=x and e^(ln x)=x only for x>0.

Use exact exponent recognition before numerical calculator evaluation; do not confuse a logarithm with multiplying by its base.

Log intensity scales compare ratios: Delta magnitude = log_10(I1/I2), not the absolute intensity itself.

The parent y=log_b(x), b>0 and b!=1, has domain x>0, full real range, vertical asymptote x=0, and x-intercept(1,0).

For y=a·log_b(c(x−h))+k, solve the complete argument positivity constraint first; the asymptote is at the argument zero whenever c!=0.

Replacing x by −x reflects a logarithmic graph over the y-axis and changes its domain. A negative multiplier reflects over the x-axis.

Horizontal translations change logarithmic domains and vertical asymptotes; vertical translations do not change full real range.

Graphs of b^x and log_b(x) reflect across y=x; use independent points and graph reasoned features.

Before solving equations combining logarithms, restrict every argument to be strictly positive. Verify candidate roots in the original equations.

For any valid common base b, log_b(MN)=log_b M+log_b N, log_b(M/N)=log_b M−log_b N and log_b(M^k)=k log_b M, with all original log arguments positive.

Expand products and quotients after identifying positive variable restrictions; when condensation creates an expression, preserve original domains.

Use roots as rational exponents. For positive x, log_b(nth_root(x))=(1/n)log_b(x).

Any base b>0,b!=1 can be converted: log_b(x)=ln(x)/ln(b), for x>0.

For logarithmic equations, combine logs first, solve, then check all original argument domains and reject extraneous roots.

Translations.Title: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations
Translations.Explanation:
Exponential equations with common positive base b≠1 are solved by equating their exponents: b^S=b^T iff S=T.

Rewrite powers to a common base when possible. When bases are different use ln on positive sides of the equation, apply log power rules and solve for the unknown.

Exponential outputs with positive multipliers are strictly positive. Reject equations that require such expressions to be negative.

For Ae^(kt)=y with A,y>0 and k≠0, solve t=ln(y/A)/k. Always check the units for t and the sign of k.

When an equation is quadratic in e^x, set u=e^x, solve the quadratic and reject u≤0 before taking ln.

For real logarithms every argument must be strictly positive. Combine logs when needed, solve algebraically, then substitute candidates back to reject extraneous solutions.

Graphing verifies approximate intersections; numerical plots supplement, not replace, the exact equations and domain checks.

Half-life model A(t)=A0(1/2)^(t/T) holds for a positive initial quantity and a known half-life T. Solve by logarithms, respecting the physical time domain.

Exponential one-to-one
For b>0,b≠1, b^S=b^T iff S=T.
Rewrite common base first.
2^(x+1)=2^5 implies x=4.

Log inverse
log_b(u)=c iff u=b^c with u>0.
Exclude zero or negative log arguments.
ln x=2 implies x=e².

Positivity of exponential
For real y and b>0, b^y>0.
No real solution to b^y=negative.
3^x=−4 has no real solution.

Exponential decay half-life
A(t)=A0(1/2)^(t/T), T>0.
Remaining fraction r gives t=T·ln(r)/ln(1/2).
r=1/4 corresponds to two half-lives.

Translations.Title: Exponential and Logarithmic Models
Translations.Explanation:
Exponential growth/decay f(t)=A0e^(kt) has initial A0>0 and rate k, positive for growth, negative for decay.

Half-life T>0 leads to A(t)=A0(1/2)^(t/T). Doubling time for growth k>0 is ln2/k.

Newton's cooling is T(t)=Ts+(T0−Ts)e^(−kt); the sign of T0−Ts determines approach direction.

Logistic growth L/(1+ae^(−kt)), L>0, a>0, k>0, approaches carrying capacity L; time to double depends on starting point.

Fit a model to observed data by using constant ratios, constant differences, or logarithmic shape. Do not extrapolate beyond meaningful physical conditions.

With b>0, b!=1, b^t=e^((ln b)t); y=ln(x²) is defined for x≠0, while 2lnx requires x>0.

Orders of magnitude compare multiplicative factors of 10. Plot powers of ten by their common logarithms.

P(t) approaches L, not infinity.

Verify domain and recognize extrapolation limits.

Translations.Title: Fitting Exponential Models to Data
Translations.Explanation:
Regression estimates a mathematical relation from measured scatter data. Exponential y=ab^x, logarithmic y=a+b ln x (x>0), and logistic y=L/(1+ae^(−kx)) solve different patterns.

Use consistent input/output units, inspect original scatter, compute fitted predictions and compare residuals before selecting a model.

An exponential has approximately constant ratios under equal x-increments; a logarithm changes rapidly near small positive inputs; a logistic grows toward finite carrying capacity L.

Exact synthetic datasets can establish known parameters for learning, while real-world noisy datasets need fitted coefficients and residual analysis.

Use change of base ab^x=a e^((lnb)x), and for logistic capacity and half-capacity time use P=L/2 -> t=(ln a)/k.

Two-point exponential fits are exact interpolations, not sufficient evidence for real-world model suitability. State the original domain and potential extrapolation limitations.

Compare transformed input ln x and observed y.

Translations.Title: Angles
Translations.Explanation:
An angle consists of two rays with shared vertex. Standard position places vertex at origin, initial ray on positive x-axis and terminal ray after a directed rotation.

Counterclockwise rotation is positive and clockwise negative. Angles that differ by integer multiples of360° or2π are coterminal.

One radian subtends an arc equal in length to the circle radius; 180°=πrad, so multiply degrees byπ/180 to get radians.

Quadrantal angles terminate on axes; common special angles 30°,45°,60°,90° have exact π fractions.

Given arc radius r>0 and angle θ in radians, s=rθ; the geometric length is nonnegative for arc magnitude |θ|.

A sector with central angle θ≥0 radians has area A=(1/2)r²θ. Always convert degree measure to radians before applying this formula.

Angular speed ω=Δθ/Δt in rad/time; linear speed v=rω in distance/time. Convert wheel revolutions per minute to radians per time unit.

Translations.Title: Unit Circle: Sine and Cosine Functions
Translations.Explanation:
The unit circle x²+y²=1 maps each directed angle t to (cos t,sin t).

The horizontal coordinate is cosine, vertical coordinate sine; both are defined on all real angles and range from−1 to1.

The Pythagorean identity sin²t+cos²t=1 follows from x²+y²=1 and helps find an unknown trig value. The quadrant determines its sign.

Standard special angles 0,π/6,π/4,π/3,π/2 and their symmetric rotations have exact algebraic values.

Reference angles measure the acute angle from terminal side to x-axis. Use reference angle magnitudes and quadrant signs.

A radius r circle has coordinates (r cos t,r sin t). For a unit-circle carousel beginning at north, t=π/2+ωtime.
