Translations.Title: The Other Trigonometric Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Given unit circle point (cos t,sin t), tangent=sin t/cos t, cotangent=cos t/sin t, secant=1/cos t, cosecant=1/sin t.

All quotients require nonzero denominators. Tangent/secant undefined where cos t=0, cotangent/cosecant undefined where sin t=0.

Use special angles and reference angles to evaluate exact signs in all four quadrants; remember reciprocal and quotient identities.

Cosine and secant are even; sine,cosecant,tangent and cotangent are odd on their domains.

Besides sin²t+cos²t=1, identities 1+tan²t=sec²t and 1+cot²t=csc²t help infer missing values.

Tangent and cotangent are π-periodic, while other common trigonometric functions are 2π-periodic.

Translations.Title: Right Triangle Trigonometry
Translations.Explanation:
For acute angle A in a right triangle, sin A=opposite/hypotenuse, cos A=adjacent/hypotenuse and tan A=opposite/adjacent.

Cosecant, secant and cotangent are reciprocal ratios, respectively hypotenuse/opposite, hypotenuse/adjacent and adjacent/opposite.

The hypotenuse always lies opposite the right angle, no matter how triangle is oriented on the page.

For right-triangle acute angles A+B=90°; use cofunction identities sin A=cos B, tan A=cot B.

Special 30-60-90 and45-45-90 triangles provide exact side ratios 1:sqrt3:2 and1:1:sqrt2.

Use inverse sides with trig ratios to solve unknown lengths. Never round intermediate computations unnecessarily.

Angles of elevation and depression can be modeled by one or multiple right triangles. Label horizontal distances and vertical heights before selecting tangent.

Translations.Title: Graphs of the Sine and Cosine Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Sine and cosine have amplitude1, period2π, and values between−1 and1. Cosine is sine shifted leftπ/2.

A general sinusoid y=A sin(Bx+C)+D or A cos(Bx+C)+D has amplitude |A|, period2π/|B| for B≠0, horizontal shift−C/B, midline y=D and range[D−|A|,D+|A|].

The sign of A reflects about the midline. Use five evenly spaced key points across a full period to sketch an independent wave.

When A=0 or B=0 the model becomes constant and the standard period formula is inapplicable.

Cosine is even and sine is odd. Phase-shifted sinusoids require transformed input for symmetry discussions.

For uniform wheel motion, height h(t)=center−radius cos(ωt) if starting at the bottom; ω=2π/period.

Translations.Title: Graphs of the Other Trigonometric Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Tangent and cotangent have periodπ and vertical asymptotes caused by their denominators. Secant and cosecant are reciprocal cosine/sine with fundamental period2π.

For y=A·tan(Bx+C)+D and y=A·cot(Bx+C)+D, the period is π/|B|, phase shift−C/B, for B≠0 and A≠0.

For y=A·sec(Bx+C)+D and y=A·csc(Bx+C)+D, period2π/|B|, asymptotes where cosine or sine in denominator vanishes.

Secant/cosecant range consists of values at least |A| above or below the midline D; their branches do not cross their vertical asymptotes.

Use parities sec even, tan/cot/csc odd and exact identities sec²−tan²=1 and sin²+cos²=1.

Real-world tangent models may diverge at a finite angle but the physical interpretation breaks down before an infinite displacement.

Translations.Title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
Translations.Explanation:
Inverse sine, cosine and tangent return principal angles for trig ratios; sin−1 x means arcsin(x), not reciprocal cosecant.

arcsin domain[-1,1], range[-π/2,π/2]; arccos domain[-1,1], range[0,π]; arctan domain all real, range(−π/2,π/2).

Since periodic sine/cosine/tangent are not one-to-one over all real inputs, we restrict their domains before inverting.

sin(arcsin u)=u for |u|≤1, cos(arccos u)=u for |u|≤1, tan(arctan u)=u for real u; inverse-trig of trig yields principal representative, not always original angle.

Use a reference triangle and Pythagorean relation to evaluate compositions such as cos(arcsin u)=sqrt(1−u²).

Inverse-trig graphs reflect the selected principal branch over y=x; domain and range exchange.

Use arcsin for opposite/hypotenuse, arccos for adjacent/hypotenuse, and arctan for opposite/adjacent, ensuring appropriate geometric side restrictions.

Translations.Title: Solving Trigonometric Equations with Identities
Translations.Explanation:
Identities hold for all inputs in the common domain of the two expressions. Equations may instead hold only for particular inputs.

Fundamental Pythagorean: sin²t+cos²t=1; 1+tan²t=sec²t where cos t≠0; 1+cot²t=csc²t where sin t≠0.

Reciprocal: sec=1/cos, csc=1/sin; quotient tan=sin/cos, cot=cos/sin. Preserve original denominator exclusions when simplifying.

Cos and sec are even; sin, tan, cot, csc are odd, on their domains. Use these identities to transform negative angles.

Algebraic proof uses factoring, expanding, common denominators, and conjugates; checking individual numeric inputs only disproves false identities.

Replace negative input with correct sign.

Identity holds throughout common domain.
Numerical counterexample disproves but numerical agreement doesn't prove.
sin t+cos t=1 fails at π/4

Use sin2θ=2sinθcosθ, cos2θ=cos²θ−sin²θ=1−2sin²θ=2cos²θ−1. Derived tan2θ=2tanθ/(1−tan²θ) requires a defined quotient.

Power-reducing formulas sin²θ=(1−cos2θ)/2 and cos²θ=(1+cos2θ)/2 transform even powers into lower powers or multiple angles.

Half-angle formulas sin(θ/2)=±sqrt((1−cosθ)/2), cos(θ/2)=±sqrt((1+cosθ)/2) take signs from the half-angle quadrant.

Half tangent is sinθ/(1+cosθ) or (1−cosθ)/sinθ on domains where denominators and original tangent exist.

Higher powers can be reduced using cos4θ and product-to-sum; verify equality algebraically while respecting the original denominator domain.

Sign determined by quadrant of t/2.

Translations.Title: Sum-to-Product and Product-to-Sum Formulas
Translations.Explanation:
Product-to-sum: 2cos a cos b=cos(a+b)+cos(a−b), 2sin a sin b=cos(a−b)−cos(a+b).

Mixed products: 2sin a cos b=sin(a+b)+sin(a−b), 2cos a sin b=sin(a+b)−sin(a−b).

Sum-to-product: sin a±sin b=2sin((a+b)/2)cos((a−b)/2) for plus, or2cos((a+b)/2)sin((a−b)/2) for minus.

Cosine sum: cos a+cos b=2cos((a+b)/2)cos((a−b)/2). Cosine difference=−2sin((a+b)/2)sin((a−b)/2).

Use these identities to factor trig equations and compare graphs. Avoid canceling factors at zeros of original denominators.

Translations.Title: Solving Trigonometric Equations
Translations.Explanation:
To solve sinx=a or cosx=a with real angles, first check |a|≤1, determine reference angles, and list every branch in the requested interval.

Tangent has π-periodic solutions x=arctan(a)+kπ; sine and cosine have two branches per full cycle except at extrema.

On [0,2π), include x=0 but exclude 2π. For equations in sin(kx) or cos(kx), find all solutions for kx over k revolutions before dividing by k.

For polynomial equations in trigonometric expressions, substitute u=sinx, cosx, or tanx, factor or apply quadratic formula; discard roots outside the feasible range.

Use Pythagorean, quotient and double-angle identities to unify mixed trig equations. Never divide by a factor that could be zero without checking it separately.

Graphical zeros corroborate algebraic solutions but numerical samples do not prove completeness. Domain restrictions prevent spurious answers from reciprocal expressions.

In triangle and line-of-sight problems, translate given rise, run or hypotenuse into asin, acos or atan and check the actual physical configuration.

Independent Cool-down: solve sinx=−1/2, solve 2cos²x−cosx−1=0 and find ramp angle for rise2m run6m.

Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Trig solution sets
sin and cos have 2π periodicity; tangent has π.
Enumerate all in requested interval.
sinx=0: x=0,π in[0,2π).

Trig quadratics
Treat u=sinx/cosx/tanx algebraically.
Return to trig variable; filter domain and range.
2sin²x−sinx=0.

Multiple-angle equations
Solve in argument kx then divide.
k full periods can yield extra roots.
sin2x=0 has four distinct roots in[0,2π).

Translations.Title: Modeling with Trigonometric Equations
Translations.Explanation:
A sinusoid y=A sin(Bt+C)+D or A cos(Bt+C)+D models periodic rise and fall with amplitude |A|, midlineD and period2π/|B|.

Use measurements (maximum/minimum, time between repeated extrema and timing of a reference event) to fit physical temperature, tide, rainfall and wheel models.

Model time spent above/below a threshold by solving the trigonometric inequality over a single period, including correct strict endpoints.

Regular harmonic motion D(t)=A cos(2πft+φ) has frequency f cycles per unit time and period1/f.

A damped oscillation D(t)=A e^(−ct)cos(2πft+φ) has a decaying amplitude envelope |A|e^(−ct), c>0. A fixed stability/rest criterion should be applied to the envelope, not the first zero-crossing.

Seasonal trends may combine a long-term linear or exponential baseline with an oscillatory term, e.g. population growth plus a 12-month seasonal component.

For vector flights, resolve individual distances into north/east components before computing the resultant and its bearing.

T positive, use peak and midline.
T=12h tide oscillation.

Damped harmonic
D(t)=A e^(−ct)cos(2πft+φ), c>0.
Envelope |A|e^(−ct).
10(.8)^t cos4πt.

Trend plus seasonality
Mean baseline(t)+Acos(2πt/12).
A season does not force a declining cumulative quantity.
Monthly species count trend.

Translations.Title: Non-Right Triangles: Law of Sines
Translations.Explanation:
The Law of Sines relates sides to opposite angles: a/sin A=b/sin B=c/sin C for a nondegenerate triangle, A+B+C=180°.

ASA and AAS data determine one triangle. An SSA configuration can generate no triangle, one triangle, or two depending on feasibility and the supplementary angle.

To resolve SSA, calculate sin B=b sin A/a. Reject values outside[-1,1] and test both B=arcsin(...) and180°−B. Retain only triangles with A+B<180°.

A triangle has area=(1/2)ab sin C for sides a,b enclosing angle C. The altitude relative to side a is b sin C.

Applications include angled sightlines, satellite tracking, height measurement, non-right polygon components, and shadow geometry.

For physical problems, determine if angles are internal or elevation/depression, verify units and choose the geometrically feasible triangle.

Translations.Title: Non-Right Triangles: Law of Cosines
Translations.Explanation:
Law of Cosines in a triangle opposite side a and included angle A: a²=b²+c²−2bc cosA. Use SAS to determine a missing side.

For SSS measurements, find an angle with cosA=(b²+c²−a²)/(2bc), after confirming positive lengths and triangle inequality.

At A=90°, cosA=0 and cosine law becomes the Pythagorean theorem. For A>90°, the opposite side is longest.

Heron's formula uses semiperimeter s=(a+b+c)/2 and area sqrt(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) for a valid triangle.

The Law of Cosines also supports SSA feasibility by solving a quadratic for a missing third side; reject nonpositive and invalid solutions.

Applications include resultant distances between diverging vehicles, parallelogram diagonal lengths, regular polygon side chords and surveys.

Opposite side a paired with angle A.

cosA=(b²+c²−a²)/(2bc).
Check triangle inequality first.
5-12-13 gives opposite13 angle90°.

Heron's area
Area=sqrt(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)).
s=(a+b+c)/2.
13-14-15 area84.

Translations.Title: Polar Coordinates
Translations.Explanation:
Polar coordinates (r,θ) locate a point a signed distance r from the pole along a ray of angle θ from the positive x-axis.

Negative r places a point in the opposite angular direction; (−r,θ) and(r,θ+π) represent the same point, while θ and θ+2πk are coterminal.

Polar to Cartesian: x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ. Cartesian to polar for nonzero point: r=sqrt(x²+y²), θ=atan2(y,x) normalized to[0,2π).

For equations, substitute x=r cosθ,y=r sinθ,x²+y²=r². Keep the undivided equation when canceling r would remove the pole.

Lines: x=a corresponds r=a secθ, y=b corresponds r=b cscθ where defined. Circles such as r=2a cosθ correspond x²+y²=2ax.

An inequality in polar coordinates describes a region with angle and signed radial bounds. Be explicit whether r≥0 or negative radii are allowed.

Independent Cool-down: locate (−3,π/6); convert(−4,−4) to positive-r polar; convert r=6sinθ to Cartesian.

atan2 identifies correct quadrant.
(1,1) ->(sqrt2,π/4).

Polar equations
Replace Cartesian x,y by trig radius components.
Do not divide by r and silently lose pole.
x²+y²=4x -> r²=4r cosθ.

Translations.Title: Polar Coordinates: Graphs
Translations.Explanation:
Polar graphs are traced by θ varying through a selected domain, plotting point(r(θ)cosθ,r(θ)sinθ) and accounting for negative r.

Test potential symmetry across polar axis, lineθ=π/2 and pole, noting substitution is a sufficient but not always necessary test.

Circles include r=a cosθ (center on x-axis) and r=a sinθ (center on y-axis). Cardioids are r=a±a sinθ or r=a±a cosθ.

A general limaçon r=a+b cosθ (or sine) has an inner loop if |a|<|b|; a cusp if |a|=|b|; dimpled/convex forms otherwise.

Lemniscates have forms r²=a²cos2θ or r²=a²sin2θ and are defined only where right-hand side≥0.

Rose curves r=a cos(nθ) or r=a sin(nθ) have n petals for odd integer n and2n petals for even n; petal magnitude |a|.

Archimedean spirals r=a+bθ expand linearly with θ. Nontrivial curves may require numerical graphical investigation.

To locate curve intersections, solve for equal radii at a common θ, but also check poles and signed-radius alternative representations.

Translations.Title: Polar Form of Complex Numbers
Translations.Explanation:
Complex z=a+bi plots at (a,b) in the Argand plane with real horizontal axis and imaginary vertical axis.

The modulus r=sqrt(a²+b²) and argument θ=atan2(b,a) describe z=r(cosθ+i sinθ)=r cisθ. For zero, the argument is undefined.

Translations.Title: Parametric Equations
Translations.Explanation:
Parametric equations x=f(t), y=g(t) trace ordered positions as a parameter changes. They can represent curves not single-valued as y=f(x).

Eliminate the parameter algebraically, retaining any restrictions induced by exponential, logarithmic, radical or time domains.

The Cartesian locus generally does not preserve travel direction, time rate or whether a curve is traced repeatedly.

Ellipse x²/a²+y²/b²=1 has parameterization x=a cos t, y=b sin t, t in [0,2π), for a,b>0.

An infinite family of parameterizations may share the same locus with differing speed and orientation.

Parametric curve intersections need not occur at the same parameter value; compare Cartesian loci and parameter ranges.

Translations.Title: Vectors
Translations.Explanation:
Vectors in the plane have magnitude and direction, represented by ordered components <a,b> or ai+bj.

Displacement from initial P to terminal Q is Q−P; equivalent vectors have equal components regardless of placement.

Vector addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication operate componentwise; geometric addition uses head-to-tail triangles.

The length of v=(a,b) is sqrt(a²+b²); a unit vector is v/|v| when v≠0, and heading is quadrant-aware atan2(b,a).

Dot product u·v=u_x v_x+u_y v_y=|u||v|cosθ; use to determine angle for nonzero vectors.

Resolve force or velocity of magnitude r at angleθ into (r cosθ,r sinθ); resultant is componentwise sum.

Wind correction, relative motion and force equilibrium require the correct direction conventions and units.

Translations.Title: Systems of Linear Equations: Two Variables
Translations.Explanation:
A two-line system can have exactly one intersection, no solution for parallel distinct lines, or infinitely many points if coincident.

To solve by substitution, isolate one variable and substitute into the second equation.

To solve by elimination, add suitable scaled equations to remove one unknown; verify by substitution.

Translations.Title: Systems of Linear Equations: Three Variables
Translations.Explanation:
A three-by-three linear system can have one ordered triple, none, or infinitely many solutions.

Gaussian elimination adds multiples of equations to reach triangular form; then back substitute for z,y,x.

Elementary operations: swap two rows, scale by nonzero constant, or add a multiple of one row to another.

A contradiction0=nonzero means inconsistency. A redundant row0=0 may indicate dependent constraints.

Models for three categories use totals, ratios/differences and weighted sums, including tickets, money and population.

Check all three original equations and interpret physical feasibility.

Independent Cool-down: solve x+y+z=6,x−y=−1,y−z=−1 and classify conflicting scaled equations.

Three-variable solution
An ordered triple satisfying every equation.
Verify all three rows.

Preserve equivalence under row operations.
Reduce to z then back substitute.

sum=5 vs twice sum=12.

Translations.Explanation:
Nonlinear systems can have zero, one, two, four or other finite numbers of intersection points, or infinitely many.

Use substitution of a line into a circle or parabola to reduce a nonlinear system to a one-variable polynomial.

Elimination can solve systems involving sums/differences of x² and y².

Graph inequalities by drawing a dashed boundary for < or > and solid boundary for ≤ or ≥; shade only satisfying regions.

For a system of inequalities, the feasible set is intersection of shaded regions, which may be empty.

In a financial model profit is P(x)=R(x)−C(x); positive profit requires P(x)>0 on feasible quantities.

Translations.Title: Partial Fractions
Translations.Explanation:
A proper rational function with factorable denominator can be expanded into partial fractions according to irreducible factors.

For distinct linear factors use A/(x−a)+B/(x−b). For repeated linear factor (x−a)^m include every power denominator 1 through m.

For irreducible quadratic q(x), use linear numerator Bx+C; repeated powers q(x)^m require a separate linear numerator at every power.

Clear denominators and equate polynomial coefficients or substitute convenient roots to solve for constants.

Check decomposition by recombining and preserving every original denominator restriction.

Improper rational fractions first need polynomial long division.

Independent Cool-down: decompose (3x+5)/((x+1)(x+2)); check domain and give repeated-linear template.

Independent Try It 1: Decompose (3x+4)/((x+1)(x+2)).

Independent Try It 2: Decompose (2x+5)/(x+2)².

Independent Try It 3: Decompose (x²+4x+7)/((x+1)(x²+4)).

Independent Try It 4: Decompose (x³+2x²+x+2)/(x²+1)².
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Distinct linear
A/(x−a)+B/(x−b).
Separate factor coefficients.
Denominator(x+1)(x+2).

Repeated factor
Include all inverse powers.
A/(x−a)+B/(x−a)²+...
(x+1)².

Irreducible quadratic
(Bx+C)/q(x).
Numerator degree less than 2.
x²+1.

Method: Clear common denominator, match polynomial coefficients.
Answer: 2/(x+1)+1/(x+2).

Example 2: Repeated linear

Method: Clear common denominator, match polynomial coefficients.
Answer: 2/(x+1)+1/(x+1)².

Example 3: Quadratic factor

Method: Clear common denominator, match polynomial coefficients.
Answer: (3/5)/(x+1)+((2/5)x+13/5)/(x²+4).

Example 4: Repeated quadratic
(x³+4x²+x+4)/(x²+1)².
Method: Clear common denominator, match polynomial coefficients.
Answer: x/(x²+1)+4/(x²+1).

Parabolic reflectors place receivers at focus; p=radius²/(4depth).

Translations.Title: Continuity
Translations.Explanation:
Continuity at a requires f(a) defined, limit exists, and limit equals f(a).

Discontinuities include removable holes, finite jumps and infinite asymptotes.

For piecewise functions check left and right formulas and assigned boundary value.

Polynomial functions continuous everywhere; rational functions wherever denominator nonzero.

The intermediate value theorem applies to functions continuous on a closed interval.

Translations.Title: Derivatives
Translations.Explanation:
Derivative f'(a)=lim_(h→0)[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h when finite limit exists.

Power rule (x^n)'=n x^(n−1) and linearity differentiate polynomials.

Differentiate reciprocal and radical functions within their smooth domains.

Derivative is instantaneous rate; average rate is secant slope.

A corner or jump can prevent differentiability; differentiability implies continuity.

Tangent line y−f(a)=f'(a)(x−a); applied derivatives include marginal cost and velocity.
